Centre): Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I hold in my hand sessional paper No. 55D, tabled in the house on Friday, March 11. This was brought down in response to an order of the house passed on February 16 of this year pursuant to a motion of mine asking for the tabling of certain documents. I shall try to state my question of privilege as briefly as possible, but there are one or two facts of importance which I must indicate.
Following the passing of the motion I was invited by an officer of the department concerned to go into the office of the minister to examine the file. This was not on a confidential basis. I was told that the reason I was asked to look over the file was that I might indicate any papers which were inconsequential and need not be produced. I did so. I initialed, in accordance with the suggestion made to me, all the papers which were important and which I felt should be produced; and I was assured they would be brought down.
Now that the sessional paper has come down, to my amazement some of the very important documents which I initialed are not included. I could cite a number of them; but to be specific I shall refer to one group, namely, the communications from the regional superintendent of unemployment insurance at Winnipeg to the unemployment insurance commission here at Ottawa-and I may say that there are letters in this sessional paper between officers of various departments and their superiors at corresponding levels. The only difference between the documents produced and those withheld is that most of the documents produced approve the action taken, while those withheld disapprove.
I am sure Your Honour will agree with me, as will the Prime Minister and leader of the house, that an order of the house should be complied with, and that this sessional paper should be supplemented to such an extent as to give the full information required by the order of the house.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: COARSE GRAINS
subtopic: OATS, BARLEY AND OILSEEDS    SUPPORT PRICES FOR 1949-50 CROP YEAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to advise the house of certain decisions which the government has reached in regard to floor prices for oats, barley and oilseeds. Before dealing with the policies which the government will implement for the crop year 1949-50, I would like to make some general observations.
There has been a general easing of the world grain and oilseed position as production of grains in Europe returned close to pre-war levels, and as substantial increases were made in the production of oils and fats in that area and elsewhere. Supplies of wheat and feed grains in exporting countries during the present crop year are sufficient to meet demand, and, in spite of the prevailing financial position, most importing countries are going to secure supplies of grain which they require. As I shall indicate later, supplies of vegetable oils generally are more than adequate to meet existing demand, and in the case of certain vegetable oils, international surpluses exist today due largely to wartime expansion in production. These are basic factors which the government has had

Coarse Grains
to consider in connection with the crops under review.
I would now like to refer specifically to oats and barley. It is important that producers in the prairie provinces should continue to maintain a sound diversity in the crops which they produce, in order that there should be a corresponding diversity in the grain which this country will have for export during this period of adjustment in the world demand for, and in the world supply of, grains.
As members of the house know, western wheat producers are assured of a minimum price of $1.75 per bushel basis No. 1 northern in store Fort William-Port Arthur or Vancouver until July 31, 1950. In view of this established level of wheat prices, the government feels that producers should have reasonable assurance in respect to support prices for oats and barley during 1949-50.
The government has decided to support the price of western oats and western barley during the crop year 1949-50 at the same support prices that are in effect for the present crop. These prices are 61J cents per bushel basis No. 1 feed oats in store Fort William-Port Arthur and 90 cents per bushel basis No. 1 feed barley in store Fort William-Port Arthur. As in previous years, the Canadian wheat board will administer the support prices for these two grains. I want to emphasize that these are support prices only, and producers will have the advantage of whatever higher prices prevail during 1949-50.
In regard to oilseeds, the government must take a realistic view of the position as it exists today. Our major contact with the international oilseed position on the export side is through flaxseed. In 1948 flaxseed production in Canada amounted to 17-4 million bushels as compared with an average of 1-5 million bushels during the 1935-1939 period. Nineteen hundred and forty-eight production of flaxseed in the United States, traditionally an importer of flaxseed, is estimated at 50 million bushels as compared with an average production of 11 million bushels during the five years prior to the war. This expansion in acreage and production of flaxseed in Canada and United States has more than offset decreased production in the Argentine. It is now evident that all three countries will have surplus stocks of flaxseed or linseed oil available for export at the end of the present crop year, and of course additional supplies will be available through 1949 production.
I should say a word in regard to rapeseed and sunflower seed. There is practically no demand for rapeseed or rapeseed oil in Canada, and, as a result, this crop is almost entirely an export commodity and is there-
fore affected by the broader oilseed position which I have described. Sunflower seed is in a different position, being an edible vegetable oil which can be utilized in Canada. In my opinion sunflower seed oil will continue to have a good market in this country, and for that reason will not require continuing government support.
Under the circumstances the government is not prepared to encourage the production of oilseeds by establishing support prices for 1949-50. The position will be examined again at the beginning of the next crop year.
The government does not propose to provide specific floor prices for oats and barley produced outside of western Canada. In the opinion of the government, the interests of eastern producers marketing these grains as grain will be protected through support prices established for western oats and barley, which constitute the main stream of commercial supplies in this country.
It must be emphasized that the great bulk of oats and barley produced in eastern Canada and British Columbia is consumed on farms where grown, and does not enter into commercial channels except through livestock and livestock products. Not more than 100,000 bushels of oats and barley in eastern Canada are inspected and graded under the provisions of the Canada Grain Act, which indicates that the purely commercial movement of these grains is relatively unimportant as compared with farm consumption, and of course as compared with the commercial movement of western grains.
To the extent that eastern oats and barley are sold commercially, the producers concerned have a geographical advantage in that their prices are based broadly on the laid-down price of western grains at various points in eastern Canada. This statement is true even after allowing for the free freight policy which has been in effect for some years. There is nothing to indicate that producers in other parts of Canada who have oats and barley to sell commercially will not continue to have a price advantage, owing to the cost of shipping western oats and barley into local markets in eastern Canada.
With eastern production of oats and barley tied in closely with farm feeding, a very serious problem would arise if for some unexpected reason prices fell below a support level made effective in eastern Canada. The only practical way in which the Canadian wheat board or any other agency could implement floor policies in eastern Canada or in British Columbia would be to take delivery of these grains in carload lots in terminal positions. In this case feed grains would have to be shipped to . areas where

required 1 or purchase under a price support program. The results would be to draw off feed grain supplies from areas in which they were required to maintain the existing livestock population. The subsequent redistribution of these supplies of oats and barley purchased by the organization responsible for maintaining support prices would be a difficult and costly undertaking. Should it be found that the floor price policy that I have outlined does not in fact protect the price of oats and barley grown in eastern Canada, means will be sought to remedy the situation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
maintopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS
subtopic: WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCES
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE TO CERTAIN BENEFICIARIES
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for giving me notice of his question. I should like to make the following answer.
It has become desirable to augment the benefits payable in certain cases to beneficiaries under the War Veterans Allowance Act, and steps are being taken to do so. In most cases the beneficiaries will be the now ageing veterans of world war I.
War veterans allowance recognizes in legislation the presumption that battle service does or may result in pre-ageing, even when no pensionable disability is incurred. In May, 1930, the act provided $20 per month single and $40 per month married. In 1940 these sums were raised to $30 and $60 respectively. In 1948 they were raised to $40 and $70 respectively.
Evidence before the veterans committee of the House of Commons in 1948 was to the effect that these rates were probably too low to meet the needs of some of the beneficiaries who had no other source of income. It was pointed out that this was a condition which was particularly likely to apply in the cities. During the interval between sessions my department made a survey of the situation. This survey established the fact that a per-

Inquiries of the Ministry centage of urban dwelling war veterans allowance recipients with no other income were suffering real hardship. To meet this problem a substantial sum is included in the main estimates now tabled to be used to alleviate these conditions of hardship. Only those who are in receipt of the maximum war veterans allowance, and without other means of support, and who are unable to manage, will share in this fund.
Regional offices of the Department of Veterans Affairs are familiar with, or will discover, these cases of special need. Reasonable flexibility will be provided by regulation to make the fund operate quickly and effectively. Each case will be dealt with on its merits. Advantage will be taken of the close co-operation already existing between the Department of Veterans Affairs welfare officers and local welfare agencies. Every case investigated will be sympathetically considered in terms of the local situation. Help given may be temporary to meet an emergent condition, or it may be on a monthly basis while the special need continues.
In no instance will the supplementary grant exceed $120 per annum single and $180 per annum married. This meets in these cases the most generous increase suggested by any national veterans organization, that is, $10 per month single and $15 per month married. Regulations governing the administration of the fund are now being prepared. When completed they will be submitted to the governor in council and tabled when approved. It is planned to begin payment at an early date after the item in the estimates provided for this program shall have been approved by parliament.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned last evening I had pointed out that the government had given hon. members no assurance that they were following policies which would enable them within a year, by bringing about adequate production of the articles under control, to be able to abandon these wartime controls they are maintaining on 
our free peacetime economy. Further I had suggested that this debate gave us an opportunity to require from the government statements as to their production policies in connection with steel, housing and the certain articles of food still under control. As a third point I had asserted that the Canadian people do not want controls over various articles they need, but that rather they want adequate supplies of those commodities now in short supply, and that particularly they want and urgently need adequate housing. These five wartime controls which the government seeks power to continue are not a coherent policy. Rather, Mr. Speaker, these five controls stick out just like five sore thumbs, showing the Canadian people where the government has fallen down in stimulating the production of those things we require. For instance, steel control indicates that the government, which has had absolute control over the steel industry for many years, has failed to ensure sufficient manufacturing capacity to meet our demands and, in the alternative, has failed to obtain from foreign sources the amount of steel required to make up the shortage in the domestic supply.
The remaining price controls are very interesting. They number thirteen; and if you examine the commodities still under control you find that none of them is necessarily in short physical supply. You find that each of these remaining price controls can be traced directly to another government policy and, in particular, to another government control. There is a perfect illustration of how certain controls breed other controls. Of these thirteen price controls, eight are on fruits and vegetables and are the direct result of the government's import restriction program. If there were no import restriction program, there would be no need for any of these controls. As a matter of fact, each of these commodities had been decontrolled and controls were restored when the austerity program became effective.
Of the remaining five, two of the controls are on sugar and molasses. The reason for the maintenance of these two controls is that this government still persists in state trading. We had a debate upon this subject in the house last year in connection with sugar control. We were promised by the present Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew), who was then parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance, that it was likely that state trading in sugar would stop with the end of 1948. We find that control still being continued, however, and presumably state trading is still being continued. The people who provided us with sugar for so many years before the war are not permitted to carry out their usual function.

The remaining three controls, namely on bread, butter and flour, are designed to offset shortages which I suggest are not caused by the war, but are shortages directly resulting from the personal control exercised by the Minister of Agriculture over the agricultural policies of Canada.
The two controls on rent and priorities are simply an admission of the failure of the government in the housing field. To a great extent, they are designed to insulate the Canadian people from the administrative failures of this government. I want to confine the remainder of my remarks to the question of rent control and housing production because, as I was stressing last night, the manner in which the government is failing to stimulate the production of houses is going to lengthen the time during which rent control will be necessary.
First of all, let me assert my belief that proper legislation in respect of rent control is still necessary. So long as we have the acute shortage of housing that exists in the country today, and so long as the government's policies are such that people are not encouraged to build rental housing, it would seem to me that the need for control may continue for a considerable time. This does not mean that rent control is good. It does not mean that it is the sort of thing we want to see perpetuated in our economy. It is a necessary evil. Any government which has to request an extension of that kind of control five years after the war has not conducted its housing policies in the way the Canadian people expect. Because such a control may be necessary, Mr. Speaker, that does not preclude criticism of the measure, nor does it make it a holy thing which one must not touch.
Last night the member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) attempted to frighten me, I think, with the bogey that if I was against rent control I would not be re-elected. A threat of that kind, Mr. Speaker, is nonsense. It is not that I am against rent control now. I do not fear rent control at this moment under these circumstances. What I do fear is a government which will sit down on its most important responsibility. This government has put us in real danger of perpetual rent control, and that is the thing I do not want to see. I do not think the member for Vancouver North wants to see it. I am sure there is no one in Canada, either landlord or tenant, and certainly not one of the homeless veterans, who wants to see rent control go on for ever.
I am not raising bogeys when I suggest perpetual rent control. I imagine all the members of this house have received within the last few days a pamphlet which discloses
Transitional Measures Act that France has had rent control since some date during the first war, and has been unable to get rid of it during the many years since the first war. I say the time has arrived in this country when this rent control, which is still necessary to protect tenants, is working great hardships and great inequities upon many landlords in Canada. I think this control is deterring the construction of rental housing, so that the minister of reconstruction will be called upon for redoubled efforts in the rental housing field. I suggest it is distorting the natural distribution of housing in this country, and is putting a price premium on recently vacated or new housing accommodation. The new accommodation is not under control and the result is that the supply is limited and its cost is out of reach of most of the Canadian people who want homes.
Furthermore, this control is creating difficulties between controlled landlords and post-control landlords. I suggest to the members of the house, and particularly to the members of the government, that rent control cannot go on for ever in its present state. Each year the housing shortage continues and the need to protect people in the lower income group remains; each year the injustices against landlords grow. The time is coming, and it will not be too long delayed, when these injustices will be so great there will have to be a revision of this control. Landlords as a class, Mr. Speaker, are not the sinister type of top-hatted individual that many members of the party to my left and some members of the government would like us to believe. A large number of the landlords in this country are entirely dependent upon the earnings of their houses and apartments for their livelihood. A large number of them have sunk their savings in housing accommodation so that they might have an income for themselves in their old age. Many of the people in this class known as landlords, whom one might envisage as rich men, as a matter of fact occupy a suite in their own apartment building and do the janitor work themselves.
From that class of people we have a continued stream of correspondence complaining not simply against low rents but against the fact that the whole burden of this control is being placed on their shoulders, and that they are finding it difficult to make ends meet under it. All these people have been squeezed between fixed rents and doubled costs of fuel, repairs and living expenses and they have found it necessary to defer repairs and to do a minimum of decoration and renovation of their places. Now they are beginning to see new, modern apartments springing up probably in the same districts in which their own

Transitional Measures Act are located, and they are naturally fretting against a control which they see is designed against themselves alone.
It is under those circumstances, Mr. Speaker, that the government come in, without a word of explanation of their resolution and without any attempt to recognize and remedy these injustices of which I speak, and ask simply for continuation of this control. I think hon. members of the house should examine the case a little bit more closely than that. The government have offered us no housing production policy, nor, by way of amendment to the rent control measure, any scheme which will preserve rent control to do the necessary work that it must do and yet will ameliorate these injustices of which I speak. The government's policy apparently is simply one of frank admission of failure and a request for the continuation of controls.

Here is the situation, Mr. Speaker. The government asks for the continuation of this control for one year. Yet the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters), speaking on January 29, is reported to have said that, if he achieves his target of houses for this coming year, it will not begin to solve the housing problem. Without further explanation that seems to me to be just a warning that this measure is really not for one year, that the government are not on top of the housing problem, and that if we do not require something more from the minister than we have already had we shall be faced next year with the same debate, the same problem and the same injustices.
I want to say to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply that there is only one answer to this vexing problem of rent con-

trol, namely, the production of many more emits of rental housing than he at present contemplates. I suggest to him that the government must not be content just to count as a discharge of their responsibilities an annual increase in an inadequate program of housing. Rather they must set their sights much higher than that. If the minister thinks that on present supplies of material and labour he can see one hundred thousand houses completed in the year 1949, and if that number of houses-even though it is more than last year's supply-will still do little to bring about an adequate supply of housing for the Canadian people, he must set his sights much higher. He must double his target; he must say, if you like, two hundred thousand houses. Then if he fails in reaching an adequate target, he will have measured his failure and he will not have that anchor to windward upon which to fall back, namely, that he has achieved the target that he set for himself.
I do not think that two hundred thousand houses is a target that the minister would be foolish to shoot at. I think that a target like that is one which the Canadian economy might come close to reaching if it were given the proper incentives by this government. I suggest to the minister that he reconsider the target of one hundred thousand houses, that he calls upon industry not to be satisfied with a small increase over last year in their production of building materials, and not to be satisfied with their present plant, but to create new capital plant so that a much larger supply of building materials can be produced.
I suggest to the minister that a larger program would require a much greater supply of skilled labour in the building trades. If he has not in Canada a supply of skilled labour able to meet a much larger program, there is a good way in which he can find those new people. He can find them with their skills already developed and can bring them here; and he can train more under vocational training schemes. If he really wants to do so, he can vastly expand the production of building materials and of houses much over any target he has at present. But if he is to do that, if he is to step up his target to something which would really satisfy the Canadian people, there is one further thing that will be required of him; it is that he give to the construction industry, and to those private firms whom he will be asking to increase their investment in their capital equipment, a feeling of long-term assurance of a sustained demand for housing. If he can do that, and if he can get the Canadian business firms which are engaged in this type of production to believe that this

demand for housing will not be over this year or next but rather that it will go on through the years, I think he will get an adequate response from Canadian business and that he will surprise himself as to the target which he can really achieve.
In order that he may give Canadian business that assurance, all that his government need to do is to stop this policy of a controlled and restricted economy, reverse it completely, and give to private business in this country the assurance that, through all the lifetimes of those who now manage those affairs, there is to be an ever-expanding economy in Canada, with more people, more business and a greater production all through the years. If the government will give to the building trades that assurance of a longterm sustained demand, they will get all the housing they need, and they will get it quickly.
Before taking my seat I should like to make two further suggestions to the government. The first is that rental control and housing should be placed at once under one minister, and I suggest it should be the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters). In my view we should bring the two sides of this housing problem together-the production side and the control side. If the minister who is responsible for the production of housing will accept responsibility for rent control as well, then I suggest we will have one member of the government who really feels his responsibility in respect of housing, with all its difficulties.
At the present time the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) administers the dead hand of rent control, and the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply is responsible for housing. There is very little opportunity of bringing home to the Minister of Finance the difficulties in connection with housing, or of bringing home to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply the problems being created under rent control through the failure of the government to attack the housing problem promptly and successfully.
I believe it would be a good thing if the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply had to answer landlords and tenants as well as homeless people, particularly veterans. I believe his headaches over rent control would spur him on to a much greater effort in the field of housing.
The second suggestion I would make is that, even though controls should remain, landlords must be given some immediate relief. If rent control is to be of prolonged duration, if it is to be continued throughout this year and probably next year, then let us bring it out in the open, regularize it and 29087-94

I suggest the house has a responsibility toward that class of Canadians as well as toward any other, and must see that landlords are no longer singled out to carry the full burden of subsidizing rentals for the government-because that is what they are doing. Mr. Speaker, the resolution which the house is now debating provides that it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor in council for a limited period during the national emergency arising out of the war. I draw attention to the words, "certain orders and regulations of the governor in council."
The only explanation the house has received as to the nature of the measure the government seeks leave to introduce is in the brief statement drawn out of two ministers, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) on February 7. In support of a measure as important as this one, we have had very brief statements which were literally wrung out of these two ministers. One of them said in effect, "this is to continue five types of controls", and the other minister

Transitional Measures Act spoke briefly about Ms plans with respect to the controls coming within the jurisdiction of his department.
It is clear from their remarks, particularly those of the Minister of Finance, that the bill is to be one to which certain orders in council will be annexed, and that the house will be asked in blanket fashion to give statutory effect to orders in council. In other words, the method pursued in previous years by the government with respect to this type of legislation-an altogether wrong method-is to be continued again, if the house will submit to it. And I urge that the house ought not to submit to a wrong method of legislating.
There are three obvious features to this resolution. The first is that it contemplates the present existence of a national emergency, and that the orders and regulations should be continued as long as the national emergency continues, within the time limit proposed in the bill to follow.
I do not wish to labour this point, because it was dealt with in such a masterly and comprehensive fashion by my esteemed leader yesterday, and I think it is crystal clear and needs no further elaboration. I simply mention that where one finds controls as varied as those referred to by the two ministers in their brief statements, it is not enough from the constitutional and legal point of view simply to make a general recital to the effect that a national emergency exists. Particularly in view of the latest judicial pronouncement on the subject by the Manitoba court of appeal with respect to establishing the existence of a national emergency in connection with a particular problem with which the legislation seeks to deal, the course the government is taking is not adequate. This judgment holds that with respect to each of the problems referred to it is necessary that the existence of a state of national emergency be established in order that validity may be acquired for the legislation the house is asked to adopt.
The second obvious feature is that the house is simply being asked to continue existing orders in council. It is not being given the opportunity of proceeding in the proper and normal legislative fashion, and of following parliamentary methods through the submission of a bill containing detailed provisions which the House of Commons, in obedience to its duty, would review before giving the bill three readings. The house is not to be given that opportunity.
This inherently wrong method is again being pursued. We will simply have orders in council handed to us and we will be told to approve them, lock, stock and barrel. That

simply is not good enough. If it cannot make up its own mind as to what to do in connection with detailed1 provisions of orders in council, the minimum the government ought to have done was to follow the procedure the house insisted upon when in the 1946 session the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) introduced a bill to give legislative approval in general terms to an order in council having to do with reinstatement in civil employment.
What the house insisted on at that time was that the bill should not be given second reading but that the subject matter be referred to the special committee on veterans affairs. That committee, instead of reporting the order in council to the house, wrote a proper bill. Surely if this government is capable of learning a lesson it should have learned that lesson, and learned it long ago. I shall have something to say about the orders at a later point.
The government is now asking us to continue the vice of delegating power. First, tMs house is being asked to delegate in a sense legislative approval to orders in council, and then the orders in council themselves will delegate great and sweeping powers to certain boards and officials, particularly one board. That is an inherently wrong method. In 1949, nearly four years after V-E day, I submit that there can no longer be any justification for asking this house to legislate in that holus-bolus fashion.
If the house does permit the bill to be introduced in the form contemplated, and I hope it will not, I trust the government is not going to attempt to do what it did in 1947 with the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act. When that measure was first introduced the government did not even set out the text of the orders as an appendix to the bill. Reference was made to them only by number and this house had no opportunity of confirming the text of the orders to which it was being asked to give legislative effect.
The third obvious feature of this resolution is the multiplicity of subjects which is embraced within its scope. We were told by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), as reported at page 316 of Hansard, that it is to continue five types of control. First, price control over certain commodities; second, rent control; third, steel control and price control over steel; fourth, timber control; and, fifth, priorities control.
May I recall to the house what happened two years ago when the government introduced a similar omnibus bill which was characterized by the same looseness which characterizes the method being followed by the government in connection with the pres-

ent resolution. At that time the government sought permission to introduce a measure to give omnibus approval to no fewer than fifty-seven orders in council. Thank goodness we are not being asked by this inherently wrong method to give legislative approval to so many orders in council, but nevertheless the same principle applies here. The house must assert its adherence to principle unless it is content to lie down and let this government steamroller things through as it has in the past.
Hon. members will remember the significant words that were spoken in 1947 in the debate on that measure. I hope the house has not forgotten the memorable speech delivered on that occasion by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power). He drew attention to the inherently dangerous method of legislating in that omnibus fashion. He drew attention to the duty of the house to scrutinize a resolution of this kind before giving approval to the introduction of a measure to be based thereon. Significantly he recalled the storm of protest which the Liberal party, under the former Prime Minister who was then leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), raised in 1932 to a relatively simple resolution introduced by the then Prime Minister, Mr. Bennett, in which two subjects had been linked together. Those subjects, unemployment and farm relief, were clearly related, but the rafters rang with the indignant protests of the right hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Mackenzie King) at what was said to be an invasion of the rights of parliament.
That same party now seeks to repeat the monstrous imposition upon parliament which was perpetrated by it in 1947. May I recall to you the closing words of the memorable speech delivered on March 20, 1947, by the hon. member for Quebec South, who had this to say, as reported on page 1595 of Hansard of that date:
My last objection is that, by passing this resolution and bringing in the bill, in the shape in which it will be brought in, we are creating an extremely dangerous precedent. We are preparing the way for the time when any government or a government which will not have the same respect for ancient constitutional usages and practices will be in power in this country, and when they come in they will have ready-made at their hand such legislation as will enable them at once to put into effect their theories and the practice in which they believe.
I have said before and said many a time that I have no objection to a great many of their theories. I would like to see many of them put into practice if they could do away with the regimentation that goes with them. But I certainly do not want to be a member of a party which will prepare the way and make it easier for them when they do come into power to carry out what I believe to be false principles in a democracy. In other words, I do not want to be a St. John the Baptist for a socialist messiah.

There seems to be a loud outburst from the hon. gentleman to my left. If he wishes to indicate his sincere devotion to a principle which is inherently wrong he will have an opportunity in due course.
I drew attention at the outset of my remarks to the fact that the government has not attempted to offer any alternative policies. The government has not attempted to put into force any policies which would eliminate the necessity of dealing with questions of this kind, policies that would get to the root of the matter and deal with the problems. Instead we see an impotent and useless government slithering around the problems in the slipshod fashion that has characterized its continuing adherence to power. The government has always been ready to use existing problems as an excuse for requesting the continuation of sweeping arbitrary powers rather than trying to cure the problems.
That is the fundamental accusation I make. That is the fundamental difference between the Progressive Conservative party and this government in connection with measures of this kind. The government have not attempted to grapple with the problems; they have ignored the problems. They come now to the house and ask to be clothed with arbitrary powers, using these problems as a pretext. The problems themselves should be grappled with and solved by proper legislative practices and administrative policy on the part of the government.
We are told that certain orders and regulations are to be continued. What are these orders and regulations? We have some idea because of the imposing residue, I may say, that remains of the orders to which

The socialist members to the left, Mr. Speaker, will also have to justify their support of a measure that will give the wartime


prices and trade board power to reimpose wage controls and salary controls.
Let me pass on to section 8, which puts upon the person charged with a breach of the order the onus of proving that he has not committed a breach of the order in respect of the price at which he sells his goods. That is entirely undemocratic. It is just as antithetical as anything can be to the things we are supposed to stand for in this Canadian parliament. I submit to the house that if it has retained its sense of duty and sense of self-respect it cannot possibly approve measures of that kind. One may go through the other orders that will be continued by the bill to follow, if the house permits it.
Order No. P.C 9029 again gives sweeping powers to the wartime prices and trade board to enter any premises, and examine any books of people whom they suspect of having committed any breach of the leasehold regulations. No warrant is needed; they can just walk into premises and take over the books. That is the kind of legislation that the government is asking us to continue under the guise of giving them power to deal with a particular problem. The problem is there, of course it is; but it ought not to be made the excuse for arbitrary and high-handed methods of that kind.
There is a similar criticism of the order on steel control, P.C. 245. With respect to steel that order contains some of the most sweeping provisions that the mind of man could devise. Under section 3 of that order the steel controller can take possession of steel wherever he finds it. He can enter on any land, and into any mine, plant, factory, mill and other buildings for the purpose of inspecting operations. He can enter on, take possession of and utilize any mine, land, plant, factory, mill, refinery, smelter, foundry, warehouse, building, or place that is used or capable of being used for the purpose of producing or dealing in or with steel, and other things in relation to steel. In the year 1949 is this house going to justify the continuation of powers as sweeping as those? The situation that exists cannot, by any stretch of a reasonable mind, be treated as an excuse for the continuation of powers like these.
There is a similar situation with the order establishing timber control, P.C. 1997. The timber controller has power, among many other things, to enter on, take possession of and utilize any land or premises or any plant, building, place, equipment or facilities used or capable of being used for producing and/or dealing in timber. He can produce or deal in timber; he can do many other things. There is nothing in the situation today that justifies a continuation of vast powers such as these.

A similar provision exists in the order dealing with priorities, P.C. 1609. Do the members of the house realize that section 2 of this order gives the priorities officer power to prohibit the making of, or dealing in, construction materials? It does not stop with giving the priorities officer power to control and regulate the making of or dealing in construction material; he has the power to prohibit. Any good citizen who is interested and engaged in the production of these materials should know that it will lie within the power of the priorities officer to step in and to prohibit him from continuing his operation if these orders are continued in force in their present form.
Running through all these orders there is that vice, to which I drew attention earlier in my remarks, of the power to delegate power, to delegate to officials power to do many things under these orders. They are powers that no self-respecting House of Commons can contemplate being conferred by it upon officials.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that these orders mark again the determination of the government to retain power that is centralized at Ottawa, the kind of power that the C.C.F. want to see centralized here. Again, in a measure of this kind, the C.C.F. see eye to eye with the Liberal party. The C.C.F., in the program it laid down at its convention last summer, advocated again the appointment of a national planning board. They want to see the constitution changed in order that power can be concentrated in a national planning board and thus control the economy of the country. They want to see the constitution changed in order that there may be vested in the government power to regulate all trade and commerce. It is all of a piece with the proposals of the league for social reconstruction in the book they put out in 1935, "Social Planning in Canada", when they advocated the establishment of a national planning board of three or not more than five persons to plan the economy, a vision of a super-centralized Canada. To the extent that the C.C.F. can see in this measure the fulfilment of their hopes-and they can see a good deal in it-they will of course applaud it and support it to the limit.
Again, Mr. Speaker, measures of this kind, seeking to continue powers that cannot be justified in the face of present conditions, powers that go far beyond the needs of the government to deal with existing problems, are definitely socialistic. Those are the controls the C.C.F. want to see made permanent, and of course the government is very obliging.
I have spoken about the continuation of wage control made possible by this measure.

It is so interesting to see the hon. member coming to the rescue of the government. How he does love to find himself in bed side by side with the government opposite. All I have to say to him is that he is welcome to it; we want none of it.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in the time that remains to me I wish to comment briefly on one or two other matters. The subject of housing has been dealt with already by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt) in his constructive contribution to the debate. It was made quite clear by my leader in his remarks yesterday that an adverse vote on this omnibus resolution by any member of this party is not to be considered as opposition to rent control, a proper statutory measure of rent control. That has been made abundantly clear by the observations of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) at pages 1446 and 1448 of Hansard yesterday, so let there be no misunderstanding of the attitude of the members of this official opposition, of which I think we had a veiled suggestion last evening in the question asked by a member to your right, Mr. Speaker, on the subject of rent control. It has to be a proper measure; it has to be a measure in proper statutory form, not something hidden in an omnibus resolution of this kind.
The government has made a sorry botch and failure of housing, which was the subject of some of those juicy promises on which they got themselves elected in 1945. May I here express publicly to my esteemed and hon. friend the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters) my profound sympathy, in that his admission to the charmed government circle should have been on the basis of his acceptance of such a lemon as was fobbed off on him by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). That minister, having made one of the most lamentable failures in Canadian government history in dealing with this housing problem, now passes it off on the unsuspecting Minister of Reconstruction and Supply. I wish to say to the minister in all sincerity that in anything I have to say on the subject of housing, either in this house or elsewhere, I shall have due sympathy for the unhappy position in which he now vicariously finds himself.
Not a word has fallen from the lips of a member of the government this session as to how they are going to cope with the housing crisis. When I spoke in this house on February 3 during the debate on the speech from the throne, I quoted figures indicating that according to statements made by leading government officials the housing crisis in Canada is just as serious today as it was three years ago. Our net progress in three

years under this administration has been absolutely nil. Put that fact, Mr. Speaker, against those juicy promises which the government held out to the people in 1945.
What are they doing to encourage the people who have accommodation in the form of one room or two rooms that they would be prepared to rent if it were not for the freezing controls which apply to shared accommodation? What are they doing about that? We argued this question at great length two years ago. We asked the government to eliminate the freezing controls from shared accommodation as applied to tenancies thereafter created. The government, of course, turned a deaf ear to anything in the form of a constructive suggestion. Apparently, they are content that the problem should continue.
We will never see a solution of this housing problem, of such critical proportions in this country, so long as there is manifested on the part of this government such a smug and self-complacent attitude as was exhibited in this chamber last night when the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) crowed about eighty-one thousand houses. I should like to say to him, and to any other member of the government who shares his smugness in the face of the critical housing situation, that the people of Canada know the government has made absolutely no progress in three years, with all its boasting and blustering, and has failed lamentably in the discharge of its duty to the people of Ganada.
In the short space of time that remains I cannot say all I had intended to say. I shall close with this observation. There are many things the government could do to meet the problem of inflation, because we have inflation in Canada. One of the things that is so obvious, and to which the government closes its eyes, is the matter of money supply. Taking the last issue of the statistical summary of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Speaker, one can see that within the last four months the money supply in Canada, which is controlled by the Bank of Canada, is higher than it has ever been in the country's history, $4,500 million. All through 1948 the money supply has increased out of all proportion to the rate of increase in industrial and commercial activity. Is it any wonder that all through 1948 the dollar has gone down in value and the price level has risen? There is something to which the government could address itself, if it had the courage and energy to do so.
There is one place where the government could make a most effective and constructive contribution towards meeting the problem of the Canadian consumer, the high cost of living and the higher scale of taxation; but will the government do anything? They have
Transitional Measures Act turned a deaf ear to the pleas that have been made for tax relief, pleas that have been made on behalf of the suffering Canadian people. The government has chosen for itself the role of oppressor of the Canadian people by continuing its extortionate taxes which cannot be justified in times like these.
We know it is part and parcel of the communist strategy to foment a depression in the free western countries wherever it is possible. It is part of their scheme to bring about chaos by the advent of the depression. They have been working for that, Mr. Speaker. Did it not shock you then to see a statement recently made by the member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold well), which is quoted in the Montreal Gazette dated December 31, 1948? Ottawa, December 30: C.C.F. leader M. J. Coldwell admitted here tonight that there was little possibility that Canada would have a "democratic socialist" government in the immediate future unless the dominion entered a period of economic distress.
You know now, Mr. Speaker, who wants to see economic distress in this country because of the political advantages it would give them. It is the duty of the members of this house to assert that they will be true to their responsibility to the Canadian people and work in this house for such proper and constitutional measures as will contribute to the lasting prosperity, happiness and freedom of the Canadian people.

I have sat here now for the better part of two days and listened to seven Conservatives stand in their places and sing the same swan song. I think it is time the tune was changed. In my opinion, the tactics being employed are designed to stop the introduction of the bill. Every argument they advanced, from the leader to the last gentleman who spoke, this little merchant of the spoken word, it was the same story. It has been a straight argument on behalf of big business and the protection of capital. The basis of their argument is that capital has a prior right over the rights of the human being. The government has no right to enter the picture to protect the rights of the little people.
The hon. member who just spoke went out of his way to antagonize people. I think it is unbecoming, you know, because I like him. At one time, I told him that if I were ever being tried for murder, he would be my lawyer. He asked me why, and I said, "For the simple reason that I would die of old age before the case reached the jury." I do not

The fact of the matter is that all the government is requesting in the bill that will be introduced, because it is similar to the bill we passed last year, is this: They want to give statutory protection to the little fellow who is renting a home today but who will be on the street a week from Monday if this measure is not passed. When this bill becomes effective, in so far as rent control is concerned, all it means is that those who are renting accommodation, who have not a home of their own, will not be evicted for one year.
