speechtext: The control within is such that all of the economic processes of the country, by means of which the people live, are in the hands of one small group. The hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross), who is a farmer-and T have seen him stand up and wave his arms- knows that the price of practically everything produced on a farm today, from milk right down, is fixed by the packing companies of this country from coast to coast. That is price fixing. They make the money. They milk the farmers. That is price control; that is irresponsible control from the outside, responsible to no one. Who fixes the price of fuel?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Who set the price of wheat?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is it fixed by the government?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: John L. Lewis.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Certainly it is not fixed by the government. It is fixed by Dominion Steel and Coal in the east and by Canadian Collieries in the west. They will charge you, and you pay through the nose. You have no say in what you pay. That is price fixing. That is control from the outside. That situation ramifies through the whole economic set-up. Pressure from these groups can force your government into doing the things they want done. In both the provincial and federal fields, I am reasonably sure that from time to time cabinets are in the position of wrangling with these pressure groups against certain proposals that are not in the best interests of the Canadian people. That is control; that

Transitional Measures Act is the kind of control that my friend the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) wants. I am not surprised, because he does not come from the stratum of society where he has been up against that kind of stuff. But if he ever becomes a cabinet minister he will know what it means. Or if he ever works for one of these corporations, comes to a conference table, and attempts to negotiate wages, he will know what is meant when it is said that there is no humanity in industry. I have been told that. I have been told that figures on the right side of the ledger are what count, that this is a business proposition. The corporation will use you as long as they can wring profits out of you. That is the kind of industry that I have been hearing about in the last seven speeches. I have been hearing a plea for these poor fellows who today actually have in their hands all of the power in this country.
When I hear hon. members in this house talk about democracy, and Saving our democratic set-up I am afraid that, if they do not smarten up and try to re-establish democracy in this country, they may do what has been done in Europe-that is, pull the house of cards down over their ears. That is the kind of thing that has happened in Europe. What we have in this country today is not the democracy that was established by confederation. What we have is a managerial form of society. The government is managed from the outside, and that would be much more the case than it is today if my hon. friends to my right were over on the opposite side. I believe however, that those on the opposite side today are really trying to struggle against that sort of thing. At least they are going this far; they are saying: "We are going to maintain rent control so thousands of people in this country will not be evicted". My hon. friends sitting to my right say "Take them off, and let them be evicted".

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No, no.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is not so.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: You are dead wrong.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
An attempt is being made to maintain some price control on flour, citrus fruits and other things of that kind. But my hon. friends to my right say, "Take them off; let flour go up. We stand for the milling companies, so that they will make more money."
Then, in the matter of housing, the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) gets up about every second day and wants to know where he is going to get nails.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: And I am still wondering where I am going to get them. If that is a priority of the government, under controls-

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: But when we had controls the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply could get up every once in a while and tell him where to get them.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No, no. I have the priorities as to where they went.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: But today, under private enterprise-no nails.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is government misdirection.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Then, has not housing been in the hands of free enterprise since the end of the war?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No; it is under national housing.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The government set up some machinery. They took more responsibility than they should have taken when they were not handling it themselves. The fact is that the government guaranteed the money to the lending companies, established the National Housing Act, and placed it in the hands of the insurance companies in the matter of administration-and we get no housing. Then hon. members to my right scream at the government because they are not getting houses. Why? Because free enterprise cannot produce. They are not building the houses. Let me repeat what we have said on a good many occasions, that we will never have houses in this country for the low-income groups until subsidized housing is established; and they will never be built until they are built through the municipalities and towns, where they can do the planning for themselves in their own communities, and where they have the administrative machinery to do it. And unless it is taken out of the hands of the insurance companies which want to make money out of it, we will not have any houses.
Then what is the position of free enterprise in connection with steel production? Someone will say there is steel control. That is true, to some extent. If there were not, I do not imagine we would have much steel in this country. The government provided for the extension of plants, and pleaded with free enterprise to do something about it. But free enterprise did not do much. Then the government came along with a fifty-fifty proposition, whereby it would provide half the capital. Still not much was done about it.
There is an example of the failure of free enterprise, where it had failed to supply the necessary quantities of steel in this country- something basic to our whole economy. I say that, when controls were taken off the whole structure they should have been

retained for at least some years, until we got back to a peacetime economy. That was a wrong procedure, and is responsible for the condition we face today.
I do not think the people for whom hon. members to my right have been pleading are suffering much. I happened to pick up the Ottawa Journal this morning and I find that International Nickel reports a. net profit of $5,604,938 higher than last year. The article states:
International Nickel Company of Canada, Limited, had net profit in 1948 of $39,108,404, up $5,604,938 from 1947.
This is after setting aside $3,000,000 for contingencies and is equal to $2.55 a common share, compared with $2.16 in 1947.
Of the profits, $29,156,338, or $2 a share, was paid in common dividends and $1,933,899 in preferred. Balance of $8,018,167 was retained for future requirements of the company.
One could look at the records of any corporation in this country and get the same kind of figures. But if one stands in the House of Commons and says, as in the case of International Nickel, that the man who went down into the mine at Sudbury, threw his body against nature and sweat that wealth out of the ground, is entitled to an equal share of what he produced, and that capital has no prior right over him, one is branded as a socialist or a communist-or dangerous, as one of my colleagues has suggested.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Or it is regimentation.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I was listening to the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) who, I notice, has now left the chamber-and I do not blame him.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: He can't take it.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: After reading about these International Nickel profits, having some idea of what the men who go down in the mine are up against, and after listening to this accusation of socialism and communism, and what have you, I happened to pick from my files this document which, it seems to me, is an answer to this nonsense one hears spoken about socialism. This is humanitarianism.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It is Liberalism.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
With a small 1. I just happened to pick this up while the hon. member was speaking. It states:
Labour is prior to, and independent of, capital. Capital is only the fruits of labour, and could never have existed if labour had not existed first. Labour is the superior of capital, and deserves much the higher consideration.
Where do you think that came from? If I were to ask that of the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Skey) he would likely say it came from "Who Owns Canada", or some other C.C.F. publication. Abraham Lincoln
Transitional Measures Act said that in December, 1861. We see just how far back my hon. friends are. The language we talk today Abraham Lincoln was talking away back in 1861. That is the right of the human being to share in the wealth he has produced; the right to a home and all it stands for.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Jesse James.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
He was a gentleman; at least he took a chance.
I had not intended taking part in the debate, until the hon. member for Eglinton provoked me. I should like now to conclude, in the hope that we may get around to the bill and make a study of it. I hope it contains much more than it did last year, and that the government is reimposing many of the controls which were taken off. I suggest they ought not to take too seriously much of what they hear from the official opposition, my Progressive Conservative friends, because the official opposition is not talking the language of the people of this country. There is one thing the people understand today, and it is that the government took them through the war by a process of planning the economy of the country. They protected the income of the people by means of price controls and subsidies. Through excess profits taxes a fair share of profits was taken from industry. If the government were to reimpose these controls tomorrow it would be backed by 75 per cent of the people of this country. I suggest that serious consideration be given to that before the next election takes place.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, now that my good friend the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) has disposed, at least to his own satisfaction-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Of the Tory party.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
-of the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and other members of the Progressive Conservative party, I would ask the patience of the house for a few moments while I deal with what seems to me to be the fundamental question raised by this debate. I suggest the question is this: Is Canada in 1949 to have parliamentary government or emergency controls? The resolution under discussion reads:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor in council for a limited period during the national emergency arising out of the war.
This measure is the great-grandchild of the War Measures Act. As hon. members know, that act permitted the government to take almost any step by order in council during the war. There was no serious quarrel

Transitional Measures Act with such a measure under war conditions. Then in 1945, when the fighting had ended, the government brought in what was called the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act. That act gave to the government much the same powers that had been exercisable under the War Measures Act. I think the act of 1945 was continued in 1946 and then in 1947 we had introduced what was called the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act. I would ask the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) to correct me if I am wrong in this outline.
The preamble of the act of 1947 referred to the fact that it was to be temporary. It was mentioned in the headnote also that the powers were to be for a limited period only. Instead of giving the government over-all powers in certain fields, the act had fifty-seven orders in council as a schedule. Your Honour will recall that it was called the Heinz bill, because there were fifty-seven varieties of order in council. In 1948 this act was extended for a period of one year so that it has remained in effect until the present time. Today we are considering its successor, the Transitional Measures Act of 1949.
This great-grandchild was ushered into the world the other evening rather apologetically. The Minister of Justice, who is sponsoring it, had nothing to say at all; he just threw the resolution on the table and sat down. Later in the debate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) got up and explained that he was to be responsible for some of the orders in council which were to be continued under this new measure, and his statement will be found at page 316 of Hansard.
He referred, first of all, to rental control. He explained that he had been trying to palm off rental control on the provinces but had been unsuccessful. He said he was now sponsoring it in this bill. He mentioned also the wartime prices and trade board and said that the price control powers granted to that board would apply only to twelve commodities. Those commodities were flour, bread, butter, citrus fruits, imported canned citrus fruit juices, certain fresh vegetables, imported onions, certain fresh fruits including imported apples and imported grapes, domestic canned vegetables, imported canned fruits, molasses and sugar. It will be noticed that over half of those commodities are imported.
Then the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) took over and explained that he was responsible for the other three orders in council which were to be retained by this bill. First was steel control, for which he 
put up quite an argument. The second was timber control, about which he was very halfhearted. He said that that control might be needed for a few months, but he was very lukewarm about it. I understand from British Columbia that the timber control is now of little effect and it would make practically no difference if it were dropped. The third was the priorities control and, like the timber control, the minister said that it would probably be required only for a matter of a few months.
I think members of the government realize that they are not on very firm ground in asking for a continuation of these emergency powers. That may be one reason why so few members of the government are speaking in this debate. Another explanation may be a statement which was made by the Solicitor General (Mr. Jean) last November. I have here a press dispatch reporting an interview given by the minister in Quebec on November 24. It was carried by the Canadian Press and reads:
Order In council rule era ending.
Solicitor General "hopes" no need now for cabinet's wartime power.
Quebec, November 24-(CP)-Solicitor General Jean said here Tuesday at a press conference that possibly the last use of procedure by order in council under Canada's emergency transitional powers act has been made by the federal cabinet.
Mr. Jean said he is due to present in Ottawa today his final report as head of a committee on application of the emergency powers.
He said he hoped there will be no further necessity for cabinet orders under the legislation designed to ease the country from a war to a peacetime administration footing.
Mr. Jean made the statement during a meeting with newspapermen.
His discussion of administration by order in council was in reply to a question whether the Liberal party was concerned about criticism that the authority of parliament had been supplanted by the cabinet.
Mr. Jean said he happened to be in charge of a committee appointed to take charge of the question of returning to parliament administrative power which during the war had been assumed by the cabinet.
It is quite obvious that even last fall the Solicitor General realized the weakness of trying to maintain these emergency powers, but apparently he has been overruled. This resolution is clear evidence of the failure of the cabinet to shake off their wartime mentality; it shows quite clearly that they still have an order-in-council hangover.
The problems to be dealt with by this measure are important and they are difficult.
I admit that they are very serious. I think those problems might be summed up as the rental problem, the prices problem and the steel problem. They are much too important to be trifled with, to be left to order in council and regulation under a minister and controllers, deputy controllers, assistants and so-

on. They are much too important to be dealt with on an emergency basis. They are really much too deep-seated to be solved by temporary measures. After all, this bill must be considered as a temporary measure whereas permanent remedies are required. The fundamental error in the government's planning has been that it is basing the legislation on war emergency.
Let us take the rental problem first. That problem arises out of a great shortage of housing. There are many reasons for a shortage of housing. In the first place there was a failure to build homes during the 1930's. Then, of course, there was a failure during the war, and we have had a great increase in population since the war. Many thousands of people have come to Canada from abroad. Another reason is that there has been a movement from the farms and rural areas to the towns and cities. I am quite sure that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) will not contradict me when I make that statement. I believe that the shortage of housing is growing worse each year; in other words, that buildings are not being put up as fast as the demand arises for new homes. Obviously, therefore, the problem will be with us for many years, and it is one of the most serious facing Canada today.
I must say that I think it is also obvious that rental controls cannot be lifted at this time. Such action would result in great suffering, particularly in the cities. Certainly in the very large cities of Canada that would be the case. There should be a clear-cut, definite policy on rental control set out in statute form. If that were done responsibility for the measure would be placed directly on the members of the house rather than on controllers and wartime prices and trade board employees across the country. If rental control were set out in statute form it would give certainty where there is none today for either the tenant or the landlord.
As hon. members know, control today is by order in council and regulation, subject to chopping and changing. Every so often a change comes out. One change benefits the tenant, the next change benefits the landlord, and neither the tenant nor the landlord is sure of his rights. I think the present situation is unfair to both of them. They both have to run to the rental control officers. Lawyers very often do not know what the regulations are, and there is great uncertainty.
I think the greatest uncertainty of all is caused by the fact that no one knows, either in this house or across the country, whether the government intends to stay in the rental field or to get out of it. Apparently the government tried to get out last fall. Now is the time for the government to decide. If it
Transitional Measures Act intends to vacate the rental control field a year from now, in 1950, the decision should be announced in order to give the provincial governments an opportunity to pass legislation establishing provincial rental control should they feel that is wise, and also to set up the administration to look after those provincial controls.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: They have had that chance already and did not care to take it.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, the member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) is not quite right in that statement. The government said in effect, "if you want to take over rental controls we will get out of the field", but what provincial premier would walk into that trouble if he did not have to? I am sure if the member for Vancouver North were premier of British Columbia he would not be in a hurry.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I would think that the premier of Quebec and the former premier of Ontario, who are so exercised over provincial rights, would have gladly moved into that field.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is really not a question; it is a speech.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: They want all the privileges and none of the responsibilities.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The point I am making is this. If the government intends to get out of the rental control field in April, 1950, for goodness' sake make that announcement now, or very shortly, so that proper steps can be taken by the provincial authorities. There is another reason why the position should be made clear. Old age pensioners, in British Columbia at least, have been very hard hit by rentals. One of their main problems is to get a house for which they can afford to pay the rent. There are now different service clubs helping to build homes for the senior citizens, which homes rent for a very small fee. They should know well in advance if the control is to be taken off so that plans to help in the construction of these homes can be speeded up.
On the other hand, if the government is not going to vacate the rental control field, then permanent legislation should be passed bringing rental control in line with the dominion housing legislation, tying it in with the present legislation designed to increase the number of homes.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
What about butter
control?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
In any event, no matter what stand the government takes on rental control.

Transitional Measures Act certainly leadership should be given by the dominion in setting up a low-rental housing scheme for Canada. The initiative for such schemes must come from the dominion.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
What about butter
control?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Just about a month ago the premier of British Columbia was reported in the Vancouver Sun as follows:
The provincial government will take part in a joint dominion-provincial-municipal conference to be held this year on a plan for low rental housing projects, Premier Johnson announced in the legislature.
I was very pleased to read that announcement, but a few days later a question was asked in the house by the member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), and the reply he got from the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters) was to the effect that there would be no such dominion-provincial-municipal conference, but that the dominion would be willing to talk the question over with individual provinces, and I think he also said with municipalities. That is not good enough; that is not going to bring about any low rental housing schemes.
I am afraid that the difficulty is the attitude of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) towards the question. He was quoted on October 28, 1947, as having said in Montreal: "Subsidized housing threat to democracy"-St. Laurent.
The dispatch reads:
External Affairs Minister St. Laurent said Monday night "no government of which I am a part would ever pass legislation for subsidized housing." He was replying to a question during a speech to the McGill university Liberal club. Affable, pleasant and apparently happy as he discussed the rise and flowering of Liberalism in Canada, Mr. St. Laurent leaped to his feet during the question period with his answer to the problem of how soon subsidized housing would make its appearance in Canada.
"Not while I am there," snapped the minister as he cut off the hardly-heard questioner. He declared he believed it unconstitutional and a threat to democracy.
Much the same attitude was taken by the Prime Minister a few days ago in his speech in "The Nation's Business" series on the radio. He is reported on March 4 this year as having said with regard to subsidized housing:
I am very definite, however, in my belief that the initiative in providing low-rental housing for civilians should be taken either by the provinces or by municipalities empowered to do so by the provinces.
That does not show much of a tendency to take the initiative in bringing about a low-rental housing scheme. Actually since 1935, when the late Right Hon. R. B. Bennett placed the Dominion Housing Act on the statute books of Canada, the housing legisla-
tion has been taken to include low-rental housing schemes, and I repeat that the initiative should come from the dominion.
So much for the rental problem. Now I should like to say a word about the second matter to which I referred; that is, the prices problem. The wartime prices and trade board is now practically gone. It is to be given power only over twelve commodities. So whether we believe or do not believe in that board, the fact is that to all intents and purposes its effectiveness has ended, and certainly it will be quite unable to keep down the cost of living during the year that lies ahead. I think the wartime prices and trade board is to be used largely as a bluff in an attempt to keep prices down; in fact I think that has been the main function of the board in the mind of the government during the last year. Many of these commodities which are to remain under the jurisdiction of the board are imported, as I said a few moments ago, and control over those articles can be maintained by virtue of the export and import permit legislation, which is permanent.
Here, too, on the question of price control, there is need for a long-term policy; and I think the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) should study the possibility of setting up adequate control over such things as illegal combines. The government seems very slow in carrying on prosecutions under that act. The machinery provided by that legislation does not seem very effective. Another direction in which thought should be given to permanent legislation is that of keeping the flow of goods at all times free in Canada. We have such things as the withholding of new patents. Improvements are being made; yet under our patent laws it is possible to keep those improvements off the market. That is a field in which the Department of Justice could do a great deal of good, and I think it could do much to keep down prices. In Canada various other unfair practices are indulged in by a minority, not by a majority of the people. The vast majority of Canadians are honest and trying to play the game with their fellow citizens, but I think we do need a tightening up in such legislation.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Such as monopolies.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Yes; where there are unfair monopolies they have to be dealt with, too. There is a field for permanent legislation, and I suggest the Minister of Justice should be giving attention to matters of that kind.
The third matter I mentioned was the steel problem. That is not a war emergency. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) explained on January 28 of this year how the steel prob-

lem arises. At page 67 of Hansard he used these words:
The defence of Canada is a matter of federal jurisdiction at all times; the defence of Canada requires watchfulness and preparation at all times. Steel is an indispensable material for the proper organization and maintenance of those forces which it is the responsibility of the central government to keep in existence.
He based the proposed actions of the government in connection with steel on national defence. Really it was worry over a third world war rather than an emergency arising out of the second world war. And there is to be legislation on steel. I point out to the Minister of Justice that the speech from the throne promises:
-legislative provision for governmental assistance by loan to the producers of basic steel for the purpose of increasing production.
Why cannot the minister include in that steel legislation the provisions required for steel control, instead of leaving them in order in council form? If that were done parliament would be given direct control over steel. The order in council which this measure will keep in force gives to the steel controller and all his henchmen absolutely dictatorial power over the steel industry, including such things as the mining of iron ore. I would refer hon. members to the interpretation clause of that order in council, which defines "steel" to include all steel products, iron ore, iron metal, alloys of iron and carbon, with or without other metals, any raw materials and minerals excepting coal and coke which go into the making of steel and also any scrap metal. It provides further that the minister may declare in writing that any article, commodity, substance or thing may be included or excluded from "steel" for the purpose of these regulations. The order in council also gives the controller this power:
To enter on, take possession of, and utilize any mine, land, plant, factory, mill, refinery, smelter, foundry, warehouse, building, or place or any equipment used or capable of being used for the purpose of producing or dealing in or with steel and to deal in or with or take possession of any vehicles, cars, ships, locomotives, or other equipment deemed by the steel controller to be required or useful for the operation of any such mine, plant, factory, mill, refinery, smelter, foundry, warehouse, building or place and/or for producing or dealing in steel or equipment-
And "equipment" is very widely defined.
-provided that any order of the steel controller made under the powers vested in him by this paragraph shall be subject to any conflicting valid order of the transport controller appointed by the government on the recommendation of the Minister of Transport.
The widest possible power that can be expressed in the English language is given in that steel control order; and I suggest to the Minister of Justice it is now time that we
Transitional Measures Act had these provisions in statute form, and further that it is time for a permanent steel policy.
Finally, our main objection to this measure is the fact that emergency powers are continuing. Emergency powers are dangerous. Surely the ministers must realize that. Such powers give the persons who exercise them delusions of grandeur. They forget they are the servants of the Canadian people, not their masters. I need only quote from the article by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) in Maclean's magazine of February 1, 1947, entitled "What's Wrong with the Liberals?" No one knows better than the hon. member for Quebec South what is wrong with the Liberals. Here is what he said:
During the war years we all drifted away from democratic ideas and principles. The condition was not peculiar to the one party. It cut across every element in the nation. I believe most Canadians were in accord with the process invoked to fight the war-the extraordinary steps taken, the controls, the censorship, the security powers, the bypassing of parliament, what was tantamount to government-by-decree.
And he went on:
Undoubtedly speed, efficiency, expediency and secrecy were essential in wartime. But there is no need for any continuing sacrifice of cherished liberties or democratic principles today.
Then he went on to say:
Extraordinary power does something to the people who wield it.
That sets forth our views on these emergency powers. There is a further reference contained in the book "From Smoke to Smother", by Douglas Reed. He is the author of "Insanity Fair", the book which was written before the war and which showed us so clearly what was going to happen. At page 174, he is dealing with the United Kingdom government's emergency powers, and he says this:
Under "emergency powers" power becomes irresponsible, like a high-tension cable cut loose. When individual ministers may do this or that by signing a paper, without submitting it to parliament, the doctrine of collective governmental responsibility collapses and the limits of departmental authority become blurred.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, since the opening of this session a very clear example of the dangers of emergency powers has come to my attention. Some members will recall that I raised a question in this chamber concerning what is known as the Fraserview project in greater Vancouver. That is a veterans' housing scheme under the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The objective of the scheme is worth while. It is to establish homes for eleven or twelve hundred veterans. The corporation expropriated a certain area in the southeastern corner

Transitional Measures Act of the city of Vancouver for this scheme. In that area there were between two and three hundred home owners. Instead of dealing with those home owners individually and attempting to see that they were not upset, the corporation simply expropriated the whole property, including the homes.
The expropriation plan contained a complete change of streets and lot boundaries. The corporation told these people they could have no more than about a forty-foot lot. If one had more than that, even though it was in garden or being used for chickens, it was taken away. If a person had a vacant lot in that area, that was taken too. During the time that this board has been in existence it has been a law unto itself because, under these original regulations which are still in effect, the powers granted to the board could be delegated. Certain officers of the board were given authority to issue orders and regulations, which orders and regulations would have the force of law. These officers to whom these powers were delegated have, through the years, issued hundreds and hundreds of various orders and regulations which all have the force of statute law. Mr. Speaker, just before the dinner recess I was dealing with the remarks made yesterday by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) when he read certain extracts from a judgment of the Manitoba court of appeal. Some of the extracts he read showed that the court had analysed the matter and had set forth its opinion as to what constitutes a national emergency. They came to the conclusion that there was no national emergency in the case at bar.
Through you, Mr. Speaker, I would ask the responsible minister to indicate to the house full information as to why these so-called emergency controls-with the exception of rent controls-are still necessary. A mere glance at the original orders in council clearly indicates the very wide powers given to the wartime prices and trade board. I should like to indicate briefly some of the extraordinary and in my opinion somewhat arbitrary provisions of some of these orders in council, as set out in the office consolidation of these rental regulations for February, 1949. At page 6 I find the following extract:
The board shall have power from time to time to enter any premises, to inspect and examine the same and any or all books, records and documents in the possession or control of any landlord or of his agent, and to require any such person to produce such books, records and documents at any place before it or before any person appointed by it to investigate, and to take possession of any or all of such books, records and documents.
And at pages 7 and 8:
The board may exercise its powers by order and may from time to time delegate to any person and authorize him to exercise from time to time such of the powers of the board on such terms as the board deems proper; and the signature or countersignature by the chairman of any order purporting to have been made by such person under authority of the board shall be conclusive evidence of such authority but nothing in these regulations shall be construed as requiring such signature or countersignature.
Then, in the same book, a severe penalty is set out whereby, upon conviction, an accused is liable to a fine of $5,000 and subject to imprisonment for a period not exceeding two years. At page 10, under the general provisions, there is this very interesting regulation:
Every provision of the Interpretation Act shall extend and apply to every order published or printed in the Canada Gazette or Canadian war orders and regulations or statutory orders and regu-


lations or in any extra thereof or extract therefrom purporting to have been printed by the King's Printer for Canada, but nothing herein contained shall be construed as requiring such publication or printing.
I would point out the significance of the last few words, "but nothing herein contained shall be construed as requiring such publication or printing." It seems to me that under that provision an order of the board could be passed and some regulation made by the administrator which would be binding; and it would not be necessary to have it published in the Canada Gazette or under these other provisions.
While those regulations are severe enough, I should like to refer to some of the regulations under P.C. 8528, in the office consolidation of that order in council, which deals with the immunity of all persons employed by the board. Section 15 states:
No member of the board and no administrator or other person employed or appointed by the board or acting on behalf of or under authority of the board shall be or become liable to any person for or in respect of any act or omission of himself or any other person in the exercise or purported exercise of any power, discretion or authority or in the performance or purported performance of any duty conferred or imposed by or under these regulations or any regulations for which these regulations are substituted or otherwise conferred or imposed by the governor in council.
And section 15 (2) states:
No proceedings by way of injunction, mandatory order, mandamus prohibition certiorari or otherwise shall be instituted against any member of the board, administrator or other person for or in respect of any act or omission of himself or any other person in the exercise or purported exercise of any power, discretion or authority or in the performance or purported performance of any duty conferred or imposed by or under these regulations or any regulations for which these regulations are substituted or otherwise conferred or imposed by the governor in council.
It seems to me that nowhere under any dominion statute or under any provincial statute in Canada will one find such wide and sweeping powers given to any board-a board which has authority to make orders and regulations which have the force of law, a board which has authority to delegate powers to make orders and regulations- and then, as the crowning indignity of it all, in section 15 (2) to provide that no person shall have any right of any action against any official of the board, no matter what he or she may do.
It seems to me it will be most difficult for any members in the house to vote for the continuance of such autocratic powers. I would point out that at least in Ontario there has been a wide difference of opinion as to the meaning and legality of many of the orders and regulations passed by the

board. Not only is there the judgment of the Manitoba court of appeal referred to yesterday by the leader of the opposition, where it was decided that there was no emergency, but also in Ontario we have the recent decision of the Ontario court of appeal in the McGinn case, in which it found certain provisions of the wartime prices and trade board regulations were invalid. And any Ontario lawyer who follows the law reports must have been impressed by the wide difference of opinion between judges of the county courts and justices of the supreme court as to the meaning of these various orders and regulations.
I would refer to the Ontario Weekly Notes of February 18, 1949, page 95, where a justice of the Ontario court of appeal, giving the judgment of the court in a rental appeal case, made this very significant statement:
I confess to having had much difficulty in trying to understand that section, particularly subsection 2 thereof.
In the judgment of the court of appeal the judgment of the court below was upset. In my opinion that shows, as I said, that there is a great difference of opinion among members of the judiciary as to the exact meaning of these orders and regulations.
In another Ontario case reported in the Ontario Weekly Notes of January 14, 1949, a justice of the supreme court of Ontario, giving judgment in a rental appeal case, made this significant statement, as it appears at page 4:
Looking at the matter apart from authority, one must realize even now, and despite the changes which have come about as to the extent of government intervention in private affairs, that order No. 294 is a somewhat extraordinary and arbitrary invasion of what was formerly regarded as the private business of the ordinary citizen.
I ask you to note the words of the justice where he states that the order is an extraordinary and arbitrary invasion of what was formerly regarded as the private business of the ordinary citizen. I agree entirely with what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) said yesterday when he asked the minister to bring in separate bills for each of the controls he is now asking to have continued. I think it is only reasonable that we members of this parliament should put into statute form those controls which it is found necessary to continue so that the Canadian citizen will know exactly what are his rights.
When consideration is given to the far-reaching and arbitrary orders and regulations that have been issued by this board; when consideration is given to the wide and sweeping powers conferred on the board with the additional authority to delegate those powers to other persons; when consideration
Transitional Measures Act is given to the complete immunity of the board no matter what its actions may be, I wonder how any hon. member can vote for this resolution and persuade his own conscience that such powers are in accordance with well known, well defined and well established Canadian legal procedure.
On many other occasions I have referred in this house to the manner in which the wartime prices and trade board have carried out their duties. This board has sent snoopers around the country to harass and embarrass merchants. Where one merchant will be prosecuted, the next goes free although he is guilty of the same offence. In the face of such tactics I wonder how the board can expect the Canadian citizen to respect the methods under which these regulations and orders are administered.
We have heard a lot about tenants. As a country lawyer I have had much to do with both tenants and landlords. I should like to point out that landlords as well as tenants have certain legal rights. From my own personal knowledge of many cases in my own county I have come to the conclusion that the landlord might just as well have stayed at home rather than attend the hearing for all the benefit he received.
One is perhaps inclined to forget that in the average small municipality the total revenue is derived from taxation on real estate. Taxes, replacements, repairs and everything else in connection with rental property have increased greatly. So far as labour and materials are concerned, the increase is anywhere from 50 to 100 per cent. Taxes have also increased greatly, but the landlord has been allowed an increase of only 10 per cent.
I can readily understand why the socialist C.C.F. will be ready to vote for the resolution. The socialists are all for controls and if they saw their way clear they would regiment the entire economic life of this nation. In my opinion no government can make a nation great by planned economy through controls. The sooner these socialist controls are removed, the sooner we get away from a paternal state which feels that it has to spoon-feed the Canadian people, the better it will be for the'general public.

I am going to suggest that the government reverse its policy. It has tried about everything so far- everything but letting the people manage their own affairs. I suggest that we go back for a short time to those good days when honest and competent people were permitted to look after their own

Mr. Speaker, I did not think I should let this debate go any further without putting on the record some extracts from a document which to me appears to be one of the most significant that has come into the hands of members of parliament. It reports on the experience of France where property was placed under rent control in 1914; and from that time up to the present French property has been subject to rent control. Recently there has come into my hands a document written by a Frenchman by the name of Bertrand de Jouvenel, entitled "No vacancies."
Before I put this on the record I should like to refer briefly to what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) said yesterday when referring to this matter, as reported on page 1454 of Hansard. I quote:
The emergency in regard to rental housing is entirely an emergency created hy this government. If they want to deal with that, let them do so by a proper bill that will recognize the rights of those who occupy homes and of those who own them, and will permit proper housing plans under the various controls they already have and are seeking to perpetuate.
There cannot be an urban member in this house who is unaware of the problems that face his constituents arising from the government's rental control policy. Property owners are being disfranchised to some extent and tenants are being made uncomfortable. In most cases tenants are unable to look forward to finding alternative accommodation. There cannot be an hon. member of this house who does not want to see the right solution found that will permit the landlord to have reasonable control over his own property and permit the tenant an opportunity to seek alternative accommodation at reasonable rental.
Mr. Bertrand de Jouvenel, as I said before, has written this significant pamphlet. I think I should begin by quoting his final conclusions which are to be found in a short paragraph entitled "Road to ruin," which reads:
Possibly the French example may prove of some interest and use to our friends across the sea. It goes to show that rent control is self-perpetuating and culminates in both the physical ruin of housing and the legal dispossession of the owners. It is enough to visit the houses in Paris to reach conclusions. The havoc wrought here is not the work of the enemy but of our own measures.
That is his concluding paragraph. In the foregoing pages he sets out the whole bleak history of what has happened in his country under rental control. It would be very unfair for me, Mr. Speaker, to take a stand for my

party that would not be in line with what my leader has said. I would be the last one to want to do that, knowing of the position that tenants in my city find themselves in today, but I do feel that it is my duty to call the attention of the house to this history which is written so clearly, because I know there is not a member here who wants to find the same thing happening in our country that has happened in France.
Here is a quotation entitled "Bootleg housing", which reads:
In short, rents are very low but there are no lodgings available. Nor are any being built. And practically none have been built for the last twelve years.
Here is another quotation entitled "Parisian plight", which reads:
To go into sordid details, eighty-two per cent of the Parisian population have no bath or shower, more than half of the population must go out of their lodgings to find a lavatory, and a fifth do not even have running water in their lodgings.
Here is another example:
To take an example of a very common situation, here is a lady who owns three buildings containing thirty-four apartments, all inhabited by middle class families. Her net loss from the thirty-four apartments, taxes and repairs taken care of, is $80 per year. Not only must her son put her up and take care of her, but he must also pay out the $80. She cannot sell; there are no buyers.
This is a man who has no axe to grind in our country, and in this document we can read the record of what has happened in France. That is why I should like to place myself on record as being in full agreement with the member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt) when he said this afternoon that the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters) should have under his jurisdiction both sides of the problem, not only the housing problem, positive action to obtain homes for Canadians, but also the negative side which is the controlling of rents. Only by having them both under his administration can the whole problem be seen in its proper perspective by one minister of the government.
I should like to change the course of my remarks for a moment and refer to the speech made this afternoon by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis). It was an amusing and interesting speech, but I do not believe that the theories which he advocated would be of any use in this country. He was talking straight socialism. As far as socialism is concerned a documentary record is being written for us today in another land across the Atlantic, Great Britain. I should like to refer the house to a few of the things that have been said in Great Britain so that those who read Hansard will have on record the other side of the question.

I rise to take part in this debate, Mr. Speaker, because several of the allusions that have been made by members of the Conservative party to the subject matter have seemed to me so erroneous as to reflect a misconception of some of the facts and legal principles involved in this matter. However, I should like to congratulate all of those, with the possible exception of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat, who have taken part in this debate today, on the excellent relevancy which has been preserved and in some cases even upon the force of their arguments. They were all arguments made by adults for adults, and in this respect quite different from those offered by the members of the same party in the debate yesterday. I can think of nothing which would have been more useful to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) than to be in the house this afternoon and hear the speech delivered by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming). He would have learned much about how a case should be presented to this house in a matter of this kind.
From this I would not wish it to be inferred by any means that I agree that the arguments presented by the hon. member for Eglinton were sound. Before resuming my seat I hope to deal with most of the main arguments made, by him and his colleagues. In the meantime I think the time would not be wasted if we gave some attention to the legal aspects of the question now before us.
The resolution we are considering is intended to lead to the introduction of a bill to amend the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act of 1947. The first two recitals of the preamble of that act are quite relevant to this discussion, and I should like to read them:
Whereas parliament, in view of the continuation of the national emergency arising out of the war, by the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, 1945, conferred upon the governor in council certain transitional powers, pursuant to which the governor in council has continued in force certain

orders and regulations made under the War Measures Act and has made other orders and regulations; And whereas the national emergency arising out of the war, in certain aspects, has continued since the unconditional surrender of Germany and Tapan and is still continuing . . .
When we amend an act introduced by a preamble of that sort, by substituting another section 7 providing for its termination approximately a year hence, we in effect import that preamble into what we are doing in this piece of legislation. In other words, as the leader of the opposition quite correctly stated yesterday, this house takes it upon itself to declare that in certain aspects the war-induced emergency which gave rise to the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act, 1947, then continued and is still continuing today.
That act of 1947 was quite short, containing only seven sections. The first set out the short title. The second provided that the orders and regulations set out in its schedule would continue in force. The third section provided for the employment of the necessary persons to administer it; the fourth, that the governor in council may revoke in whole or in part any of the regulations named in the schedule to the act; the fifth, provided for the publication of these orders; the sixth, the coming into force of the act; and the seventh, which we are now amending by the bill before us, the duration of the act. From the beginning, it has been on a temporary basis, renewal from year to year. It does not, therefore, present any of the dire consequences such as those envisaged by the last speaker in the case of France or Britain because the nature of this legislation from its commencement has been of an emergent or temporary character. The language is designed to carry out that idea.

The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and, I believe, the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) this afternoon, and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) yesterday, put forth this argument which, on its face, seems to have some merit. They say this. If it is desirable that these controls should be continued, why not bring before this house a statute setting forth, in terms that the members of the house can check, the provisions for that control? My reply is this. We are proposing to the house that it should continue the existing orders in council because it is hoped that the control
1504

Transitional Measures Act thereby provided is temporary and therefore it is not desirable to put the law into the form of a permanent statute. More than that, we are here dealing, and through the years have been dealing, with a situation which is not only temporary in its duration but which changes in its character quite substantially from time to time in a quite unpredictable way; and it is impossible, under a statute, to get the degree of flexibility and adaptability of administrative regulations and the like which are appropriate to deal with a problem of that kind.
During this period of economic stress or emergency resulting from war and from the shortages occasioned by war, the regulations passed under the authority of the statute of which we are now seeking the amendment required constant and frequent revision and adjustment. To have this subject to statute, which would require amendments to be brought in and passed by this house from time to time, would involve a rigidity which would be wholly inappropriate in dealing with matters of that sort. For example, since March, 1948, on this very subject of rental regulation, commercial accommodation, as we know, has been decontrolled; landlords who need their homes for their personal residence have been permitted to give to their tenants six months' notice to vacate. Any landlord, no matter when he purchases a house, may apply for exemption, based upon grievous hardship to him because of his inability to occupy the residence himself. A public institution may apply for exemption if it needs the accommodation for the extension of its public endeavours. And maximum rentals were increased from 10 to 15 per cent. This is an example in just one field alone which can be matched by similar changes in the regulations in others. To say to the people who are to be affected by regulations of this sort that no change could be made until the House of Commons was called together and passed an amendment to the statute would, I suggest, be very unacceptable to public opinion in this country.
The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) said this afternoon he had read in the speech from the throne that the government was introducing at this session a bill dealing with steel, and he suggested that the proper way to deal with at least steel regulations would be to incorporate them in this bill.
Now, sir, as I read the allusion in the speech from the throne-and I confine myself to that, for fear I might infringe upon the sensibilities of hon. members across the way, on a point of order, that I do not reveal any of my inside knowledge about bills which may be coming down later-
[Mr. Garson.l

speechtext:
At the instigation of my hon. friend. Now, this allusion in the speech from the throne was to legislation to provide for a loan to a steel concern in Canada. I suggest that the making of a loan to a corporation in the steel business, and the matter of the general control of steel, are subject matters so incongruous to each other that it would be highly improper to combine them in a single statute. And if it were desirable to bring down for steel regulation a statute to this House of Commons it would be much better to have the lending statute on the one hand and another statute governing steel regulation on the other hand, separate from each other. But for reasons which I have already given in the case of rental control, regulations of the sort I have indicated, which deal with a situation which is changing and fluid from time to time, are not in an appropriate form in a statute.
In view of the discussion which has taken place thus far, I do not think it is necessary to review the statements which have already been made by my colleagues the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), that these twelve orders in council still in force cover, first of all, commodities subject to price ceilings, second, rental controls, third, steel control, and fourth, timber control.
One of the arguments made by our friends of the Progressive Conservative opposition is that they oppose the continuance of these controls upon the ground, among others they put forward, that it is unconscionable for members of the House of Commons to declare that the state of emergency which formed the basis for the act as it was originally passed still continues.
As hon. members will recall, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) said that we must understand the terrible burden we take upon our conscience of declaring that there was an emergency in the country, as we must declare if we are going to pass this bill. Well, I agree entirely with my hon. friend. We do declare that the emergency still continues, because we are putting a new section 7 in a statute which has that declaration in its preamble. And when we put the new section 7 in, we do in effect make that declaration.
But surely, sir, such a declaration as that should not offend the conscience of any intelligent, reasonable and well-informed member of any legislature. I should have thought it was apparent to everyone that one of the results of every great war in history has always been inflation; and after the

greatest war in history, one in which there has been by far the greatest destruction of property, and by far the greatest outpouring of money in the war effort, inevitably in every country after a war of this magnitude under even the best of fiscal management there is a great increase in the amount of money in circulation, on the one hand, and a tremendous destruction of goods and services - upon which that money could be a claim, on the other. And that in any language spells inflation, basic inflation. To say as did the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) this afternoon, that he had noticed from one of the government publications that there was more money in circulation now after a great war than there had been before, and that therefore he immediately jumped to the conclusion that the Bank of Canada was in some way at fault, is to give an indication that my hon. friend simply does not understand the fiscal consequences of waging a great war.
If we have that condition of inflation then, sir, we have the type of economic emergency with which we are concerned in the resolution now before the house, and in the bill to be introduced. And, sir, that war-induced emergency has persisted after every war in history, and it certainly persists at the present time, and can be seen in various forms in every country of the world, civilized and uncivilized.
In the face of that emergency with all its maladjustments and dislocations, a necessity arises to introduce matters such as steel control and rent control, not as a matter of improvidence, stupidity and injustice but as a matter of prudence and good sense and in fairness to all the people of the country and particularly those who are not so well able to look after themselves.
From that I suggest that, far from its being a difficult thing for any man of conscience to affirm that we have in Canada today a war-induced emergency still continuing, I believe that the majority of members in the House of Commons will agree with me that the continuance of this exceptional condition of emergency, certainly at least so far as the matters which we seek to control in the measure now before us are concerned, is so self-evident that it is not subject to dispute at all.
In that respect I am most happy to have a very substantial measure of agreement even from members of the Progressive Conservative party. The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) rose in his place in this debate and gave a most excellent description of an emergency-a most excellent description indeed. It was well described, well worded and graphically portrayed, and his whole 29087-95i
Transitional Measures Act argument supports the position of the government. The hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) has taken part in the debate and he dealt with three matters in particular, one being steel. This is what he said about steel, as reported on page 320 of Hansard:
In so far as steel is concerned, steel is in great demand. Steel undoubtedly requires some measure of regulation.
The hon. member admits that it requires some measure of regulation.
For what reason? The reason is that projects of great magnitude-
Listen to this for a fine description of the type of emergency for which controls should be devised:
The reason is that projects of great magnitude, so far as this little country of Canada is concerned, have been held up for a great variety of reasons. To my mind, some of these reasons are patriotic. We had a war. We were told not to use steel while the war was on. We were told to forget, until the war was over, about our building projects requiring steel. The war consumed a tremendous amount of steel. Those charged with the responsibility for new construction requiring steel, realizing that a war requires a great quantity of this product, delayed their projects five years-yes, six, seven and eight years. The blueprints, however, were on the table. Those blueprints were worrying those who were directing the affairs of different organizations such as, for example, banks and office buildings.
Could you have a better description of the kind of situation arising out of a war in which it is advisable to declare an emergency and bring into effect the same steel control?

Perhaps in so doing I may satisfy the curiosity of the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman) who is asking me to show what has been done. The minister stated, as reported on page 317 of Hansard:
At the present time we are moving surplus primary steel, or semi-finished steel, from the Algoma Steel Company to the finishing plants at Hamilton, to the amount of about 18,000 tons per month. We are also moving semi-finished steel from the Dominion Steel and Coal Company at Sydney to Hamilton, to the extent of about 10,000 tons per month. That 28,000 tons of steel, which cannot be finished at Algoma or at Sydney, would ordinarily go for export and be finished in other countries.
I presume, to be used in other countries.
That was the pre-war history of the surpluses of those two plants. By moving that steel to Hamilton 28,000 tons per month of additional basic steel are turned into finished products.
In reply to the hon. member for Rosedale, who asks what we are doing, I say that that is what we are doing. The minister continued:
To end steel control abruptly at this time would, I am sure, reduce the production of finished steel from Canadian plants and Canadian foundries by as much as 20 per cent.
In the face of these facts, what sort of mentality is it that will result in an hon. member of this house getting up and saying that it disturbs his conscience and his intellectual honesty to be asked to declare that there is an emergency which warrants these controls?
During the course of the discussion the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) intro-


duced among other and irrelevant matters a recent decision of the court of appeal in my own province of Manitoba in the case of Nolan and Hallet and Carey versus the Attorney General of Canada. In replying to a question yesterday, the Minister of Trade and Commerce stated that the Department of Justice had instructed counsel to appeal this judgment. That is entirely correct. Therefore I do not think that it is proper for me, any more than it was proper yesterday for the leader of the opposition and for the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett), to comment upon a case which to all practical intents and purposes is sub judice. I am afraid that certain assertions and contributions by various members of the Conservative opposition, and I include the interjection just made by the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness), may be quite misleading to hon. members of this house when they either hear or read them subsequently in the absence of a statement of one or two cardinal legal principles that have a bearing on this matter.
The first of these principles is that there can be no doubt that the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, 1945, the first of the series, was intra vires or within the power of this parliament to enact at the time

it was enacted. The privy council has so held in the Japanese case, 1947 Appeal Cases, 87, which followed and applied the Fort Frances case, 1923 Appeal Cases, 695. In the Fort Frances case the privy council considered the constitutional validity of the War Measures Act, 1914, and certain orders in council made under the War Measures Act during the war for the control throughout Canada of the supply of newsprint paper by manufacturers and the price of newsprint. They also considered the constitutional validity of further dominion statutes, 1919, chapter 63, which were passed after the cessation of hostilities for continuing war control into the post-war period after the first world war.
Upon the point as to the continuance of the authority of parliament to pass laws dealing with matters arising under the war emergency after the cessation of hostilities, Lord Haldane in the Fort Frances case said, at page 706:
It may be that it has become clear that the crisis which arose is wholly at an end, and that there is no justification for the continued exercise of an exceptional interference which becomes ultra vires when it is no longer called for. In such a case the law as laid down for distribution of powers in the ruling instrument would have to be invoked, but a very clear evidence that the crisis had wholly passed away would be required to justify the judiciary, even when the question was one of ultra vires which it had to decide, in overruling the decision of the government that exceptional measures were still requisite.
Very clear evidence would have to be given to overrule the decision of the government that exceptional measures were still requisite. In the Japanese case-that is the one after the last war-the privy council considered the validity of three orders in council made under the War Measures Act relating to the deportation of persons of the Japanese race and the revocation of their Canadian nationality. The orders in council in question had been continued in force by P.C. 7414 made under section 4 of the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act. The privy council held that the orders in council were intra vires and that the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act was intra vires and also, by implication, that P.C. 7414 was intra vires.
With respect to the power of parliament to legislate as to an emergency arising out of the war, Lord Wright said at page 101:
On certain general matters of principle there is not, since the decision in Fort Frances Pulp and Power Company versus the Manitoba Free Press, any room for dispute. Under the British North America Act property and civil rights in the several provinces are committed to the provincial legislatures, but the parliament of the dominion in a sufficiently great emergency, such as that arising out of war, has power to deal adequately with that emergency for the safety of the dominion as a

Transitional Measures Act whole. The interests of the dominion are to be protected, and it rests with the parliament of the dominion to protect them. What those interests are the parliament of the dominion must be left with considerable freedom to judge.

If my hon. friend had been listening he would have heard me state that this is the judgment of Lord Wright.
Again if it be clear that an emergency has not arisen or no longer exists there can be no justification for the exercise or continued exercise of the exceptional powers. The rule of law as to the distribution of powers between the parliament of the dominion and the parliaments of the provinces comes into play, but very clear evidence that an emergency has not arisen, or that the emergency no longer exists, is required to justify the judiciary, even though the question is one of ultra vires, in overruling the decision of the parliament of the dominion that exceptional measures were required or were still required.
These clear statements of judicial opinion, as applied to the facts of the case now before us, require that we, in the exercise of our judgment with regard to the passage of the resolution now before us, need to satisfy ourselves merely that, with regard to the need for rental regulations, steel control, timber control, and the control of commodities which are under price ceilings, the state of war-induced emergency still continues. That is all we have to find.

On this matter of decontrol, I am very happy to say that I think the members on the government side, the members of our party, and the members of the Social Credit party all are anxious to get rid of these controls as soon as they can be got rid of and as soon as the economy of the nation will permit. Now turning again to the Minister of Justice and his references to this question of emergency, he read from the judgments of Lord Haldane, I think it was, or Lord Wright of the privy council. I was interested in hearing again some of those judgments on which I cut my teeth twenty or twenty-five years ago; I think the Free Press case was about 1923, or something like that. But I want to ask the minister this very simple question. Can one, by any statute or order in council, find the same emergency calling for a price ceiling on butter that calls for control on steel? To mention the thing, sir, is to show the complete absurdity of the whole business. Nor can one equally justify a dealing in coarse grains, we will say, and a dealing in lumber, saying that the same reason exists which one would use to prove an emergency.
I must make this exception. In time of war we had the War Measures Act, when it was just and right that the people of the nation should give up their individual freedom in order that as a whole they might maintain freedom. But those arguments have no application whatever at the present time.
Now I put this question. We had the War Measures Act, which gave complete power to the central authority. Then we struggled along with what we called the transitional powers acts, I think from 1945 on. I have often wondered why the government did not simply continue the War Measures Act. Let it be admitted that I am one of those who would have argued against that; but the same arguments are open to me today in saying that the orders we are continuing go altogether too far, some of them even further than the War Measures Act itself went. I do say that in time of peace there can be no justification for carrying things that length. With the greatest respect and some considerable admiration for the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), I should think he would be better pleased without such wide powers as he, or some other members of this government, or members of the staffs of this government, have under those orders.
[Mr. Smith (Calgary West).l
I make this suggestion in that regard. The government have said so often that they do not like continuing under order in council government. We learned from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) that only twelve of these orders are left, and if I heard him correctly he said some of them are quite unimportant. It does seem to me that we as a parliament should pass a statute declaring an emergency, if there is an emergency, and then state what is to be controlled. The Minister of Justice complained that a statute did not have the elasticity of an order in council. It has. All you have to do is say so in your statute. All you have to do is put in the statute the subject matter, leaving the regulatory matters to such authorities as those presenting the statute see fit. It has been done time and time again. To repeat the illustration I used a moment ago, it does not seem to me you can find the same emergency to justify ceiling prices on butter that you may to justify control over the output of steel mills.
Now then, what does all this mean? It means this, that it may be there are some things that require control. I am a little bothered about the legal aspect of the matter. With respect to rental control, and this will please my friends on the opposite side, I am not quite sure that, if we do pass this proposed statute and continue the order in council, it will be worth a nickel in a court of law. These matters belong to the provinces and it will be open to anyone, if he cares to take the trouble, to find out whether or not there is in fact an emergency in that connection. I do not think it would be very difficult of proof. It seems to me it would necessarily be proven.
With respect to some of these other matters, I am going to say that the question of the emergency is one upon which I have very great doubt. Some day, as in the Nolan case, it will be submitted to our courts for a final decision.
I promised, sir, I would not be long, so I am going to close with a suggestion that these matters be embodied in a statute, so that he who sows may reap. Surely with the experience the officials have had from 1945 to 1949, it should not be difficult to write into a statute these regulations which are needed now. It is not a large undertaking for any draftsman who is worth his salt, considering the experience the various departments have had in the operations of these orders under this nebulous transitional powers act. I think it could be done with respect to some commodities-let us take butter, if you will, as one product, or the cabbages we are now getting from Florida and which we could not get until a few days ago. The point I am

making is this. If we do put our imprint of approval upon these various orders, then at some time someone should do more than quote the speech of the member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) with respect to steel.
