speechtext:
Although the resolution in itself refers to the bill, which is to come before the house, to give permission to the government to continue certain regulations

that they have exercised for a number of years, to me the basic thing appears to be price control and controls generally. In discussing this matter I believe we should try to separate, for our own benefit, the two matters that have been more or less confused in this debate. First of all, there is the question of controls as such, and then there is the question of the abuse of powers. The critics of this resolution and of the government have been confusing those two issues by pointing out all the abuses-and there have been some; there have been enough for the government to have earned plenty of criticism-and using that issue as a measuring stick for deciding whether controls as such are desirable in this country at this time.
I do not think there is any member in this house who would condone any abuse of the power given to any government; and if the government or those to whom they have delegated powers under the wartime prices and trade board have in any way abused their powers or gone beyond the authority given to them by this parliament, I have no objection to anyone's exposing them and criticizing them in the strongest possible terms. We in this party believe that the powers delegated by parliament to the government, or by the government to any board, should be used for the purpose of serving the best interests of the people of this country. As long as that power is used in that way, we have no criticism of it. If it is used in any other way, or if it is abused in its application, we are just as critical as any member of this house.
The question has arisen whether price control or any other control is now necessary, in view of the question whether there is now an emergency or not. I do not intend to take up the time of this house to discuss at great length what an emergency is or whether we are now in a state of emergency. We could discuss that subject for a long time without coming to any conclusion, for this simple reason. When we speak of an emergency, we do not always speak of the same people. Let us remember that in this country today there are people, and there have been for many years, for whom the state of emergency has never passed. They have always been in a state of emergency. During the 1930's when we had mass unemployment in this country-

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: What do you know about it?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I wish you knew half as much about it as I do. During the 1930's when we had mass unemployment there were thousands-yes, hundreds of thousands of people-who for ten years were living in a 29087-96J
Transitional Measures Act state of emergency and the government did not do anything about it. There were many people then who would have thanked a government that took the trouble to pass some legislation to help them to find jobs and to give them a decent standard of living. They were not worrying about the government having too much power or doing too much. They were critical because the government was not doing enough. I think most hon. members in the house realize that now.
On the other hand there are today in Canada, and there have been for many years, people who have never felt the state of emergency so far as their economic lives are concerned. Now that the war is over those who find themselves in comfortable economic circumstances feel that there is no emergency. Naturally it depends on whom you are speaking for. If you are speaking for the class of people who thrive at a time when prices are skyrocketing or who are in a position to profiteer from the state of affairs in this country, as they have been for the past few years, then of course for them there is no emergency. For them there is a harvest to reap. But if you are speaking for the people who are obliged to pay the profits and who are the victims of exploitation, then for them there certainly is an emergency.
I wish now to refer to the charge that has been made and repeated so blithely this afternoon and evening by hon. members to our right to the effect that the C.C.F. is the party of control; that we should like to see the people controlled at all times, and that we should like to control everything. Nothing could be farther from the truth. Those who believe in the philosophy of public ownership or co-operative ownership are the very ones who can save this country from permanent price control. Under the present economic system this country will never get away from controls because the very way in which the present system operates invites controls. As long as you have an economic system which is based on profit, on the philosophy that the strongest should win and that the weakest should be trampled underfoot, then if there is to be even rough justice of any kind you must have a system of price control and other controls to keep the economic affairs of this country under some semblance of order. But if we change the economic base of this country to one of co-operation from one of competition, we shall slowly start to emerge from the position where controls are necessary. We shall emerge into a time when production shall be for use and when service shall be at cost. Then it will not be necessary to control prices because the customer and the producer will be the same person, as will be the distributor.

Transitional Measures Act
When, in any economy, you get to the stage where the people produce for their own use, distribute among themselves the goods of their own production, and enjoy the fruits of their labour without having to hand tribute to any profiteer, you will not need control. That is the reason the C.C.F. has advocated and advocates today, not a permanent system of price controls as a solution of our problem, but the extension of public ownership into legitimate fields, and the encouragement of co-operative ownership in all the fields in which it can be properly worked, thus letting the people of Canada work out their own economic solution.
Let us take our co-operatives as an example. There is no finer example of institutions which lay out their own destiny, so to speak, than the co-operative organizations. They are the producers, the distributors and the consumers, all at the same time. There is no reason for them to raise prices against each other, because it would be senseless to try to profiteer from yourself.
Therefore for hon. members to say that the C.C.F. is the party which wants permanent controls is simply to show that they do not understand the philosophy of this party. If we reach the point in this country where we are willing to admit that human rights have priority over property rights, and that human welfare in this country should have first priority at all times, then it will be possible for us to build our economic system to suit human welfare, and not try to twist the human element in our society to fit our economic system, as we are trying to do it today. That is the reason we must have price controls now.
The suggestion has been made by several members that, instead of administering these controls by order in council, they should be put into statute form. We have also heard from the same people that these controls appear to be self-perpetuating. Well, if I judge aright the temper of the government of Canada, and its actions in the past few years, it would be useless at this time to attempt to put into statute form what is left of their price-control program, as they themselves have announced it.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) took great pains this evening to try to prove to the official opposition that this is a decontrol measure he is placing before the house, rather than a measure of control. In other words, he suggests that the government have no intention of bringing about any comprehensive system of price controls, and have said so on several occasions, and that they are following out their philosophy in the present instance.

There is no basic difference on this question between the approach made by the government and that made by the official opposition. Let us not be fooled by the shadowboxing which has been going on in the house for the last few days. Both those parties believe in private enterprise and in letting people go ahead and make all the profits they can. That is what happens in practice, regardless of what they say. And I have no more faith in what the government pretends to do today, than I would have in the official opposition if it were sitting on the government benches.
What we are told is that they have left twelve orders in council controlling a number of things. We are given the list of the things still under control, so far as prices are concerned. An examination of the list would show that it all consists practically of either agricultural products or primary products, with the exception of steel and timber.
That is not a policy of price control. It is only a pitiful attempt at trying to appear as if they are controlling something. The government has gone down the road of decontrol. The Progressive Conservative opposition should be applauding what the government is doing, because it is the same thing they believe in. The government has destroyed the price stabilization system of this country by the process of decontrolling prices at a time when prices were still going up. Today they find themselves in the position where they are the ones to blame for the high cost of living. And they will soon be the ones to blame for the primary producers in this country being unable to obtain even the cost of production of their primary products.
In the face of that, however, the government is decontrolling instead of attempting to build a system of prices which would have some sort of relationship with each other, and which would have some sort of relationship between the prices received by the producers of primary products and those received by the ones who manufacture goods for sale to the primary producers.
Until some effort is made in this direction, it will be useless for the government to talk about controlling prices. It is not doing that; and it would be equally useless for the official opposition to attack the government or the C.C.F. in the matter of controls. Thus far the Progressive Conservative opposition has been attempting to show that the Liberal government is following certain socialist proposals. They might as well forget that approach, because it is becoming more evident than their speeches can make it from day to day that the affinity between

the Liberal and the Progressive Conservative philosophies for the private enterprise system is far stronger, and in practice shows itself in the coalition which we have out west.
The C.C.F. party in the House of Commons, in attempting to bring about a modicum of justice for the primary producers and consumers, has stood out, over the years, pleading for the government to maintain the price stabilization program they started during the war. If we have not been able to persuade them to do it, at least we will be able to stand on our record showing that we have fought for the benefit of the people, and that the combined parties have beaten us down.

speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? Is he aware that the C.C.F. was also a member of the Manitoba coalition?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I have heard that old chestnut once before.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is it not true?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No, it is not true.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It is true.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I have heard that old chestnut shot out in the house several times, and I might as well deal with it now.
At the time the C.C.F. participated in the government of Manitoba it was specifically stated at that time by the premier of that province, who now sits in this House of Commons, that it was a non-partisan government, and that he objected to the word coalition being used.
He stated also, publicly, through the press and radio, that it was a temporary set-up in order to help the war effort. It was on that elevated basis that the C.C.F. entered temporarily the non-partisan government of Manitoba. But it was not long before the C.C.F. found its good faith was being violated and found that it was not a non-partisan government, and that the motive behind it was to bring about coalition in order to maintain itself in power. There was only one thing to do; the C.C.F. did the honourable thing and withdrew from the coalition. But the other two parties found the necessity for clinging together in the interest of selfpreservation even greater than the necessity of preserving the public interest.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to take part in the debate. However the official opposition has been carrying on for the last two days, and their arguments are getting so thin -they were not very good to begin with- that I felt something that really mattered should be said. During the past day and a
Transitional Measures Act half they have spent most of their time in criticizing the attitude of this party toward controls.
I am not much concerned as to whether the present control bill passes or not, because there is so very little of useful control left, that is, control for the benefit of the common people of Canada, that perhaps a little heavier load would not be much harder to bear. As a matter of fact, if controls are removed altogether it will likely bring home to them all the sooner who are their friends and who are their enemies.
There are and there have been two schools of thought with regard to controls. There is one school, those who live by exploitation and who do not favour controls. Then there is the other school, the little fellow who is exploited and who favours controls because they are his protection. The little fellow was never protected to the extent he was when controls were in effect during the war period. Never in his life was his standard of living so high, and never was he so secure. For that reason he believes in controls. And who can blame him?
But neither the official opposition nor the government believe in controls. The government found that they operated well during the war and I think they were prepared to carry on with controls until supply was sufficient to meet demand, but they were continually being pushed by the official opposition to remove controls.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: And the farmers.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The farmers today want controls. If the hon. member will read the report of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture he will find there the strongest demand for controls ever made in Canada. The C.C.F. is not in favour of controls just for the sake of controls. We are in favour of government controls because we are convinced that if we do not have government controls we will have some other form of control. Let me demonstrate to the house what happens when government controls are removed.
As soon as a government control is removed another control takes its place. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who is not at the moment in his seat, last August wrote to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in regard to the allocation of newsprint. In the letter that the hon. member received from the minister appeared these words:
As you may know, the authority for the control, of allocation of newsprint, formerly vested in the wartime prices and trade board, was rescinded as of December 15, 1945 . . . The Newsprint Association of Canada, Sun Life Building, Montreal, now has; complete control of the allocation of newsprint.

Transitional Measures Act
Are my friends opposed to that kind of control?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
That is the kind of control they want. They want big business to control the lives of the people of Canada. I am being generous and am willing to assume that the government do not want that situation, but they have willingly or unwillingly allowed themselves to be pushed into the position of having to do that.
Only a few months ago there was an investigation by the combines investigation commissioner into the price and distribution of bread. It was found that the very staff of life of the people was controlled and is being controlled today. It was found that prices were set and that the bakeries had their own police to see that those prices set were adhered to. Are hon. members going to tell me that there is no control? Of course there is control. We believe that it is much better to have control by a government or an agency responsible to the people than by an agency not responsible to anyone but itself.
What has happened during the past few years through the removal of controls? The removal of each control has resulted on each occasion in an increase in the cost of living. Every increase in the cost of living has made it that much more difficult for the low-income people of this country to live. I have pointed out already that the standard of living of the low-income people of Canada, the old age pensioners, persons in receipt of war veterans allowances, those on superannuation and the like, is much lower today, despite the fact that in 1948 we had the highest level of production we have ever had in Canada, than it was during the war years.
What is the reason? The reason is that when the government removed controls those who were controlling prices allowed those prices to soar, or they put up prices and took away some more of what the little people had left. At one of the sittings of the royal commission on prices last autumn Mr. H. R. MacMillan of the MacMillan lumber interests was on the witness stand. When he was asked the reason for rising prices he said:
"We found that selling to the retailer at lower prices than other mills was having the effect of increasing the retailer's profit without doing anyone any good.
"My experience is that in the open market when the price is going up you can't stop it."
Just because you cannot stop it without controls, the little fellow is being squeezed to death while the big fellow is prospering as he never prospered before. There can be only one end to a society where squalor, misery, want, poverty and privation increase

at the bottom while wealth and luxury increase at the top. That is what is happening in Canada today.
My hon. friends of the official opposition say that four years after the war there is no need for controls. If there is no emergency now, why all this talk about military pacts? If there is no emergency now, if we are living in such a safe world, why have the defence estimates for this year been increased considerably over what they were last year, or the year before that, and the year before that? Let us talk sense. The world is on the edge of a precipice today. With that situation confronting us, hon. members to my right day after day have obstructed the work of this parliament.
Today the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) referred to certain things that had been done by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in the development of a housing project. I agree that they did not use that discretion in regard to property rights that they should have. There were, however, only some twenty or thirty properties involved. My information, obtained from letters received from some of the people concerned, is that the situation has been settled fairly well since the matter was taken up with the minister of reconstruction and the chairman of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. But I remember that when 23,000 people in British Columbia were despoiled of their property, the efforts of a lifetime, the hon. member for Vancouver South never raised his voice in protest.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: When was that?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: When the Japanese Canadians were uprooted from their homes and scattered right across this country from one end of its 4,000 miles to the other.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Your own C.C.F. leader advocated moving them.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: My own C.C.F. provincial leader did not do anything of the kind, and even if he did not have any democracy in his make-up my friend the member for Vancouver South cannot take that as an excuse for not having any himself.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Do you think they should not have been moved?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
They should not have been moved, but if they had to be moved then their properties should have been protected. The government of the country should have acted as their guardian and not as their despoiler. That is what should have been done. There is no democracy in a country unless there is democracy for everybody, democracy for those you do not like as well as for those you do like. That is the only democracy that is

worth while. That is the only democracy that I stand for or will have anything to do with.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: My goodness, you are worked up.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Why shouldn't I be worked up when I see people around me who just talk for the mere sake of talking, who talk for the mere sake of making an impression on the country?.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: On a point of order, I realize the hon. member has worked himself up into a fine state.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: On a point of order-

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I would suggest-

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Will my friend please sit down? I have the floor.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I would suggest that this has nothing to do with the resolution. I ask for your ruling on the point, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) has raised a point of order that the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver East do not refer to the resolution. I ask him to direct his remarks to the resolution.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the matter I was just referring to involves one of the orders in council referred to this evening by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), and it is in the resolutions that are going to be dealt with. My friends on the right, the official opposition, are very fond of criticism, but they cannot take it when it is directed at them. As I said, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that the matter before us is of very great moment to the people of Canada outside of rent control, and I am bound to say that rent control is not an unmixed blessing. It works to the disadvantage of some poor people although it benefits others. The question that is before us now is whether my friends in the official opposition want to see this legislation pass in order to protect the very few that it can protect now, or whether they want to see this legislation expire and these people have no protection whatever. They should say exactly what they want to see happen, and then the house can govern itself accordingly.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
This resolution has caused a great deal of heat and a great deal of discussion on matters that were hardly germane to the question of the continuation of the controls that are left from the old wartime control order. Housing is such a problem in the riding of York West that if I thought the proposed measure of the government would assist in
Transitional Measures Act the alleviation of the situation, believe me, Mr. Speaker, I would support it. On the subject of rent control there are a number of questions which we must ask ourselves, and on the answers to those questions judge its effectiveness. The questions are:
1.	Is rent control producing an equitable distribution of available housing?
2.	Does rent control result in the construction of an adequate number of houses for rent?
3.	Does rent control ameliorate substandard living conditions?
4.	Does rent control assist veterans to obtain houses, or other suitable living places?
5.	Does rent control channel building materials and building labour into residential housing rather than into commerce, entertainment or business premises?
On an entirely impartial survey of the housing situation in Canada today, Mr. Speaker, I think that the answer to all five questions must be no. It is for that reason that I believe that a statute with regard to housing should be enacted by parliament after consultation with the two other levels of government which are so intimately concerned with the whole matter. The control provided is not satisfactory, and that is why a statute is needed as to housing, and for these basic reasons.
In most Canadian towns the proper planning of a residential area is made impossible by the fact that approximately eighty per cent of all new houses do not pay sufficient taxes to cover the cost of municipal services supplied to them. This causes an urgency to compete for the location of industry at whatever social or locational cost; the gross overzoning for industrial land use, resulting in the enforced location of housing in industrial areas; the need for suburban municipalities of township size in order to spread taxation; the consequent inhibiting of the socially desirable small, compact communities; the imposition of excessive restrictions in "well planned" communities in order to exclude houses of low assessment; the refusal of municipalities to accept current federal offers of subsidized rental housing owing to the tax burdens which their acceptance would cause; the inequality of school standards as between school sections; and generally to make physical planning appear futile. No such complete study exists, although it is basic to planning and housing practice.
Those are the problems we face today in the housing or re-housing of our population. They are problems which cannot be solved or cured by a mere control act such as that
1518	HOUSE OF
Transitional Measures Act envisaged in this measure. These are problems which have to be worked out with the provinces and municipalities; and if there were no other reason why a dominion-provincial conference should be called, it is to solve this vital and pressing problem.
I want to give an example of what I mean. In the riding I represent there is a desperate shortage of houses, houses for veterans or low-rental houses of any description, and there is gross overcrowding and substandard conditions of living. The problem is acute. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation offered to build some two thousand houses in the metropolitan area of Toronto, of which a large number would be in the riding of West York. They wanted to build houses in groups of two or three hundred, the most economical way to construct a planned housing project, because in that way the contractor can move onto the land, set up his machinery, his sawmills and other manufacturing processes, and by this means a house can be built for much less than an individual house here and there, which is not mass-produced. The estimated cost of these houses was in the neighbourhood of $6,800. They would rent for $37.50 a month, a reasonable and justifiable price and a rental within the capacity of the average industrial worker in West York.
But let us look at what happened. Let us look at the problems involved in establishing one of these 300-house communities, and let us look at the impact of such a community upon the municipality. In an ideal community each of these three hundred houses would have an average of one and a half children of school age. For such a community this would mean 450 additional children in the school section. Assume there would be an average of fifty children per room, though I say this number is far too great. The present cost of constructing a school in the Toronto metropolitan area is around $33,000 to $35,000 per room. This would mean that if these three hundred desperately needed houses for veterans were constructed, the community would immediately have to face a capital outlay of over $300,000 just for schools, exclusive of such things as sewers, water, street lighting and all the other essential services. No municipality in Canada can withstand the impact of a shock as great as this. No municipality can exist without going bankrupt, if this sort of thing is to be allowed. A recent conference of mayors, reeves and municipal officers of the municipalities surrounding Toronto pointed this out to the officers of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and said they could not permit the erection of these houses unless some solution could be found 

to the school problem. That is a basic economic problem, and until it is solved you will get no low-rental housing where it is most needed.
I say this control measure does nothing to solve that problem. This control measure merely continues a pious hope that was effective before the shift of population caused by war industry, and the subsequent movement of industry into large metropolitan areas. The control measure has completely failed to give us an equitable distribution of the housing and the living space now available, and it has failed also to assist in the building of low-rental houses.
Now I want briefly to deal with this question of planning, but before that I want to say something about the corruption of the English language. "Planning" is one of the words that have been so basely corrupted. Because of the socialist insistence on over-all planning for the state, such things as town planning or planning for communities have a tinge of socialism they do not deserve. A modern community must be zoned and it must be planned. Other words have been corrupted as well. The word "home" has been corrupted. Instead of meaning, as it did in the early days, one's hearth, the place where one lived, the word "home" has been corrupted to mean a sort of jerry-built house, constructed for speculative sale. I think it is a pity that such excellent old English words should be corrupted by advertising in this way.
I want to mention the problem of the low-rental house. It may amaze this house, and I think it will interest the country, to know that, despite the protestations of the Prime Minister, this government is actually subsidizing housing to the extent of approximately $2 million a week. About one hundred million dollars a year is going into subsidized houses. If that were producing a solution for the veteran who cannot get a house, if that were producing a solution for the industrial worker who is moved from pillar to post and is living in cramped and very frequently in unsanitary conditions, if that money were really being effectively put to work, I for one would not complain. This is not the case and the situation has not improved. The men on the waiting list, the veterans with two and three children who are living in deplorable conditions and who are on the books of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, are just as numerous today as they were a year ago. Unless a trigovernment agreement can be made, there is very little hope that the situation can be improved.

With rental control we have developed a hatred between the landlord and tenant. I thought a letter which appeared in the press the other day was rather interesting in that it expressed this feeling which has grown up because of rent control. This is the letter:
The majority of landlords are not wealthy people -but today a landlord is apparently a despised citizen, classed with gangsters and criminals, all because he happens to have a house for which he has worked and saved and which somebody else now wants to occupy, all at his expense-namely, the tenant. The law gives it to him because there are more tenants than landlords and that means more votes.
I have had literally dozens of letters from the owners of small houses in my constituency. The owners of these houses have been unable, until quite recently, to live in their own houses and frequently the tenant is leasing a room or two for the amount of rent paid for the whole house. That is a grave injustice, Mr. Speaker, and it is one of the faults of an over-simplified control measure. It is for reasons such as these that I believe the whole problem of housing should come before a dominion-provincial conference, and the municipalities should have representation at that conference.
Whatever the constitution may be, conditions have made it necessary for the question of municipal taxation to be brought into the arena of dominion affairs. Following the first great war an intolerable condition developed, similar to the one which exists today. The sudden development of small houses mushroomed into the suburban municipalities surrounding the major cities. Eventually this resulted in demands for the necessary municipal services which, in turn, resulted in the bankruptcy of a large number of Ontario municipalities. This is an intolerable situation, Mr. Speaker, and a situation which we cannot permit to develop again. It is a situation, however, which we are doing everything possible to bring about by this very control order that is on our statute books. That is the problem, Mr. Speaker. I believe it is a problem that requires, not a blanket order but the attention of the best brains in all three levels of government.
We are not producing houses. Certainly we are not producing houses for rental purposes, and therefore we are not improving the conditions under which our people have to live. If this government, if any government, produced a workable plan, I would certainly support it. Having seen the operation of this present measure, having seen the conditions forced upon the people in my constituency, I do not and cannot support the measure as it is. It does not do the things it is supposed to do. It does not control rent. It does not provide low-rental housing and it
Transitional Measures Act does not allow the veteran to obtain the shelter which he deserves.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I do not wish to prevent a vote being taken tonight, Mr. Speaker, and for that reason I will confine my remarks to four or five minutes. I wish to call the attention of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) to one clause in the resolution as amended. As I said on February 7, there are 180,000 of these orders in council. As you know, Mr. Speaker, there are some people who are taking advantage of that because the Supreme Court of Canada has been the court of last resort. Only four of these orders in council have gone before the supreme court, with the result that only one of them has been held intra vires, by a vote of 4 to 3. There are some people who are taking advantage of that fact. The courts do not know what the law is.
I agree with what has been said. There is in the city of Toronto no land available for housing. If we only had a steam suburban service around the city, the housing problem could be solved satisfactorily. In the olden days we had the advantage of having in the city land at $6 and $8 a foot. Today out in the township of York, in the counties of York, Ontario and Peel, the city is giving a service by buses and electric cars, but we have no steam suburban service in that area. If we had the advantage of that service I think we should be able to solve the housing problem. Other large cities like Montreal have a steam suburban service.
In conclusion I want to say this about these orders in council. Nobody can know the law until it is finally determined. There are some people who have been put in jail illegally. I know of one case in which the man owns his own house. He is a soldier. I have seen some of the tenants who put electric stoves in cupboards away up in attics, and who do a great many things that a desirable tenant would not do. I believe there should be some control over them. I have seen some of the houses of soldiers and others and they cannot get into them. I believe there should be some change in the system. Some magistrates and county court judges in our city, and all over Ontario, are sentencing people illegally. I have been calling the attention of the house to this matter on several occasions. I do not wish to obstruct the passage of the resolution, because I should like to see it adopted. As I say, if we had the steam service that I have described furnishing transportation out to the townships, we would then have a method which would solve the housing problem in the way it was solved in the first great war.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
It may be said generally that we who belong to the
1520	HOUSE OF
Transitional Measures Act Progressive Conservative party are against controls unless those controls seek the betterment of our people. Unless the case can be proven that the control will, of necessity, make for better living conditions, then the control should not be put into operation. I should like to bring to the attention of the house again the point which was made by my colleague the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith), who said: How can the government show any reason for emergency powers, on which this legislation is supposed to be based, when the government combines under the resolution such diverse things as butter and steel? How can there be any relation whatsoever between the control of butter and the war? It is now nearly four years since the armistice, although we have not yet had a declaration of peace with regard to some of the enemy countries. But for all practical purposes the war has been over for nearly four years.
In place of there being a butter shortage and in place of there being some danger of butter going to untoward heights where a ceiling of seventy-two cents a pound or some other level is necessary, I am sure that the government must be far more concerned with the floor under butter rather than with a ceiling. Surely a floor is not an aftermath of the war. On the other hand, a ceiling might have been. So where does the government stand on that matter?
Then, again, I should like to refer to the question of oils and fats. At the moment there is in the world a great surplus of vegetable oils. If that is an aftermath of the war, then surely it is an aftermath which we

gladly welcome; and certainly it does not call for any controls of the nature of those proposed by the government at the present time. On the other hand, steel may indeed be something which requires control, because in the long years of the war steel was in such demand for war purposes that little or none was available except for the most urgent civilian uses. There may be a case to be made for the allocation of steel under government supervision. But how can any administration say that butter on the one hand, and steel on the other, provide an argument for the reasonableness of the legislation proposed under this resolution? It would seem to me that if the government wish to carry the people of this country with them they should set out the reasons for the proposed legislation and not put it in an omnibus resolution as they are now trying to do.
On motion of Mr. Jackman the debate was adjourned.
